scenes.goal: Join the room with a first greeting and discover the class's immediate problem.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Can a first greeting count before the learner feels ready?
scenes.learnerNeed: Hear a greeting, understand it, and answer with support.

intents: Begin the room with a real evening greeting.
Reveal that the atlas is unfinished and invite help without making help a test.

openingImage.description: An atlas waits under a cloth.

exitImage.description: The cloth lifts. The atlas is blank.

propCues.description: Rie repeats the one part you need.

scenes.goal: Give the blank route its first stable sound and written marks.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Will five small sounds be treated as too little, or as enough to begin?
scenes.learnerNeed: Hear the five vowel sounds before meeting their written forms.

intents: Set listening before explanation.
Turn the five vowel sounds into a compact system for all basic hiragana.

exitImage.description: The five marks join into the first route.

propCues.description: Only the sound you missed plays again.
A missed kana returns at the end. The rest stay done.
Keep the strokes that worked. Try the missed stroke again.

scenes.goal: Use the complete classroom handout to move the room and repair a missed instruction.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Can a request for repetition become the action that keeps the class moving?
scenes.learnerNeed: Use the classroom actions and repair phrases needed to follow a real lesson.

intents: Make the source instruction change a literal object in the room.
Create an honest need for repetition by moving too quickly once.
Treat repair language as the contribution that saved the route.

exitImage.description: Rie adds a flower mark. It lands on your first turn.

propCues.description: Rie resets one step and says it again.
One part is missing. Build the request again.
The example stays here. The homework goes home.

scenes.goal: Build enough sentence structure to read true and false route labels.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Can the class correct the atlas without turning correction into a verdict on a person?
scenes.learnerNeed: Use a small set of noun sentence frames to identify the room correctly.

intents: Turn sentence forms into a route check rather than isolated grammar display.

openingImage.description: Two room labels appear. Only one fits.

exitImage.description: A clear door frame settles around the classroom label.

propCues.description: Keep the parts that fit. Try the missing part again.

scenes.goal: Move the learner's spoken name sentence onto a desk card, then choose the first route mission.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Can the learner recognise on paper the same name sentence they have already said aloud?
scenes.learnerNeed: Move the familiar name + です pattern from speech onto a class card.

intents: Connect the spoken introduction to the same sentence on paper without testing untaught kana.
Offer three materially different ways to recover the next atlas label.

openingImage.description: Your name is on the card. One short space remains.

exitImage.description: Rie taps your name, then です.

scenes.goal: Find Xingyu and Mika's names by listening for the word immediately before です.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Can the learner find a name without understanding the whole introduction?
scenes.learnerNeed: Identify two short introductions by sound before seeing the text.

intents: Give the learner one small listening target without asking them to decode the whole sentence.
Show that listening for one useful landmark is already real comprehension.

openingImage.description: Two voices. Two empty name labels.

exitImage.description: Replay the missed voice. Listen just before です.

scenes.goal: Restore two missing links in a handwritten introduction note.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Can the learner use visible evidence without making the first guess final?
scenes.learnerNeed: Read around two gaps and rebuild the missing links.

intents: Define the evidence problem precisely without giving the particles away.
Turn the repaired note into a visible route rather than an answer display.

openingImage.description: Sophie and Ruparna's note has two gaps.

exitImage.description: The useful words stay visible. Try the missed gap again.

scenes.goal: Join an arrival exchange and recover naturally when a turn is missed.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Can speaking practice welcome someone without making recording compulsory?
scenes.learnerNeed: Take one supported speaking turn, with recording optional and progress saved.

intents: State the recording scope and make pausing unremarkable.
Show that a repaired turn still welcomed someone into the room.

openingImage.description: Aakash and Sam are at the classroom door.

exitImage.description: Aakash repeats the question and waits for your answer.

scenes.goal: Read the returned class cards, then finish the learner's own name in katakana.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Can the learner use one written clue, then connect their familiar name to its katakana sound?
scenes.learnerNeed: Read one useful clue, then hear and confirm the katakana on their own card.

intents: Give reading a social purpose before asking for reconstruction.

openingImage.description: Three class cards return. Yours is still face down.

exitImage.description: Rie turns the finished card upright beside the others.

propCues.description: The class line stays visible. Check the name again.
Rie says the name again and points from the usual spelling to the katakana.

scenes.goal: Use the selected mission skill after its teaching surface disappears, then leave a written route marker.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Can the learner use the language when the source page is no longer carrying the task?
scenes.learnerNeed: Use the same language once without the original prompt in view.

intents: Make the selected language useful in a changed situation.

openingImage.description: The support sheets close. A new route card waits.

exitImage.description: Your route reaches the card. The first lantern lights.

propCues.description: The new situation stays in view. Retry only the missed step.
Keep what worked. Fix only the missing part.

scenes.goal: Close the first class, preserve the exact resume state, and return learner choice to the wider Academy.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Can the first contribution remain enough even though the atlas is mostly unfinished?
scenes.learnerNeed: Finish the first class, save the route, and choose what comes next.

intents: Name the learner's repair and transfer as the first useful contribution.
Return control without presenting one destination as the loyal choice.

openingImage.description: The entrance arrow now points back to your route.

exitImage.description: Choose finish or break once more.

scenes.goal: Meet Henry through the dense private cipher he used to re-label the whole route, and reach the point where his careful system cannot be read by anyone else.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: When a clever tool is unreadable to the room, can the class fix the point everyone needs without erasing the maker's work?
scenes.learnerNeed: A re-labelling turn where writing one point in plain kana and giving a reason matters more than admiring the cipher.

intents: Proudly present the whole route re-tagged in his own private mark system, certain that once the key is learned the entire map reads at a glance.
Under the question, explain the whole cipher's logic instead of just pointing to the station — walk through the rule set past the human need.
Defend the key one more time, then hear the human note a beat late and concede that readable is better — his signature late qualifier landing on his own careful, unreadable work.
Genuinely admire the work, then try to actually use the map and hit the wall: he cannot find which mark is the station or where to get off.

openingImage.description: Overnight the atlas's first route has been covered end to end in tiny hand-drawn marks: doubled strokes, small hooks, single and double circles. It is dense, even, and clearly a system. A folded slip in the corner is labelled KEY in the same unreadable hand.

exitImage.description: One plain hiragana word — えき — now sits among Henry's dense marks, the first point on the route anyone can find. His cipher is untouched all around it; only one gap has been made legible.

propCues.description: Only the plain-kana label and its reason clause return for another try. Henry's dense marks around the point stay exactly where they were — editing the point never rubs out his system.

scenes.goal: Keep Henry's system as his own key while making the shared route legible, and decide how to hand the edit back to its maker without rejecting him.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Can the class edit the idea and keep the person, so the map is both his and everyone's?
scenes.learnerNeed: A stance on how to preserve the maker's cleverness while making the route usable by anyone who enters.

intents: Introduce himself and label his useful object plainly, giving the reason he builds his own tools — then catch himself sliding back toward a private mark.
Accept the edit warmly and reframe his own goal with a reason: he wants everyone to be able to read it, not only himself — editing instead of defending, late qualifier and all.

Separate editing the idea from rejecting the maker: keep Henry's system, but add a plain label because he needs to read the map in a second when he is running late — not instead of the cipher, alongside it.
Warm close that confirms the maker was not rejected: the system is fully intact, and now he too can find the station on the first try.

openingImage.description: Beside the one readable point sits Henry's pen case, each pen tagged in his own marks, and a stack of blank label cards. He turns a fresh card over and half-reaches to draw the next point in cipher again.

exitImage.description: The route now carries plain hiragana names along its line, and Henry's cipher is folded into a small labelled key in the corner. Anyone entering the room can read the route; nothing of the system has been thrown away.

scenes.goal: Meet Aakash through his confident rainy route from the station and hit the moment the place-name labels drop.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: When the labels vanish, will the confident guide keep talking, or ask for the one thing he needs?
scenes.learnerNeed: A live route problem where the place-name must be asked for, not read, and identity must be told apart from location.

intents: Arrive a touch late, wave everyone over, and launch the route from the station like a music-video narration.
Point at each automatic label in turn — the crossing, the corner, the good shop — riding pure momentum.
Recover by bravely asking a question — flawlessly formed — but aim it at identity (who a person is, where they are from) instead of location (where the place is).
Acknowledge, warmly and a little ruefully, that the learner's question — not his narration — brought the label back.
Praise the flawless question, then separate identity from location — the route needs where the place is, not who the person is — and hand over the ask-for-help frame.

openingImage.description: Rain sheets past the station exit. A route map glows on the wet glass, every turn tagged with an automatic place-name label. A puddle throws the labels back in neon — the whole street reads like a record sleeve. Aakash arrives a few minutes late, waving the class over.

exitImage.description: A single place-name label re-inks itself over the corner shop. The rest of the route is still blank, but it has its first named point again — and it came from a question, not the map.

propCues.description: Every automatic place-name label peels off the map at once and dissolves into the rain. The route is still there — the crossing, the corner, the shop — but nothing is named. Aakash's pointing finger stops in mid-air over a blank tag.

Rie uncaps a marker to write どこ on the blank tag; it runs dry precisely on the last stroke of こ. She holds up the dead marker, unbothered, and nods the learner toward the corner instead — the question will have to be spoken, not written.
The person-question fades out. Only the place-question frame stays lit — the blank corner tag and one particle slot — for another try. No English answer appears before the learner commits.

scenes.goal: Let Aakash reframe asking-for-help as the move that actually carries the route, and let the learner choose how to lead on.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Can needing to ask count as leading?
scenes.learnerNeed: A stance choice about how to carry a route forward when the labels will not come back on their own.

intents: Name asking-for-help as the thing that moved the route, and turn his eye for a place toward describing where it is rather than only naming it.
Instead of announcing the next turn as usual, hold still and hand the choice of the next place to the class — arrival-beat growth shown, not narrated.
Name asking-for-help, aimed at the right question, as route leadership, and leave the help frame with the class as a permanent tool.

openingImage.description: Aakash lowers his pointing hand. For once he isn't adding the next turn. The one recovered label holds on the corner; the rest of the street waits, unnamed, in the rain.

exitImage.description: The single recovered label holds steady on the corner. The rest of the street stays unnamed — but now the class knows the route isn't in the labels; it's in the asking. Aakash pockets his pointing hand and, for once, waits.

scenes.goal: Find the entrance to a listening path that opens on timing, not volume, and meet Mika as the one who hears it.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Can the quietest person in the room be the one who finds the way in?
scenes.learnerNeed: A clarification-request and rhythm-listening need where asking 'one more time' is the tool, not an admission.

intents: Notice there is a soft sound beneath the room's noise and invite listening rather than louder calling.
Barely speak up to ask for the cue once more and slowly, drop a sideways pitch fact, then start to retreat.
Find the entrance by holding a pause and silently counting the interval, then entering on the beat — timing, not volume.
Confirm one clean entrance was found by timing, and value quiet attention as a real way in.

openingImage.description: A new point on the atlas route stays shut behind a closed gate. Under the class's overlapping voices, a soft chime repeats at the same faint interval, over and over, unanswered.

exitImage.description: The route point lights, faintly, exactly on the chime's beat. The passage behind the gate is open now, and two overlapping voices can be heard inside it.

propCues.description: The class leans in and calls out louder, all at once, trying to force the point open. The gate does not move. The chime keeps its interval as if the shouting were not there.
Only the single interval that was missed replays, slowed, with a count marked over the pause. The rest of the passage stays where the learner left it; no English answer appears first.

scenes.goal: Use the opened passage to work out whose item is whose and request the right one, and name quiet attention as a shared class tool.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Will the class treat Mika's quiet listening as an ensemble skill, not a personality footnote?
scenes.learnerNeed: A possession and specific-request turn that only works once you have heard whose item it is, and a stance on the quiet method.

intents: Catch and be able to hum the passage's melody, but be unable to tell whose item is whose — the rhythm complement to Mika's timing.
Use the pause to place whose item is whose, then openly say he cannot read the kanji on the label and ask for its reading — naming the unclear part as method.
Accept, staying quiet, that the pause-and-count is now a shared class technique and that listening quietly is a full ensemble role.

openingImage.description: Inside the passage, two recorded voices overlap. Each names an item; each says one is theirs. A single card label carries a kanji the atlas has left unread.

exitImage.description: A small marker settles on the atlas at the opened point: not a lantern, just a mark that means listen. It keeps a steady, quiet beat while the route runs on past it.

title.ja: ラスボスは、小さな一枚

scenes.goal: Run Tom's oversized katakana game by reading the cards, counting the pieces, and following his commands.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Will the game be won by the biggest, most dramatic card, or by reading the cards at all?
scenes.learnerNeed: A live play loop that forces katakana to be read by shape, pieces to be counted, and spoken commands to be followed — with no English gloss to lean on.

intents: Unveil the game as a dramatic final-boss battle and issue the first command to start play by drawing one card.
Run the game by counting every piece for the sheer fun of it, then command the room to read the cards closely.
Admit that drawing the giant boss card, the whole centrepiece of his spectacle, does not win the game.
While the room stares at the giant boss card, quietly point out that only the smallest card carries a marker — a folded paper cat.

openingImage.description: Tom clears the front desk and lays out an oversized card game. Five big katakana cards stand in a row, three round tokens beside them. One card towers over the rest, hand-labelled ボス. On the battered game box, a small photo sticker of a dog is captioned チェスナットさん. Clipped to the smallest, plainest card at the edge is a folded paper cat, easy to miss.

exitImage.description: The ボス card stands drawn and enormous at the centre, and the game sits stalled around it. At the edge of the table, unmoved, the folded paper cat still marks the smallest, plainest card.

propCues.description: Only the card that was misread turns back face up on its own; the cards already read correctly stay where the learner placed them. No English gloss appears — just the katakana, a little larger, waiting to be read again.

scenes.goal: Let the game be settled by reading the smallest, paper-cat-marked card instead of by the biggest gesture.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Will spectacle make room for another person's quiet find, or keep insisting on the boss?
scenes.learnerNeed: A stance on who reads the one small card that actually decides the game, once reading it — not drawing the boss — is what matters.

intents: Turn the class from the giant card back to the small one the paper cat marks, and ask for it to be read by its katakana.
Take quiet delight that the small marker was the whole game, and wave off his own noticing as luck rather than skill.
Feel the pull of his own spectacle, then let it go and agree that the small marked card is the one to read.
Name the outcome plainly: the smallest card, read correctly, wins — not the biggest gesture.

openingImage.description: The class has crowded in around the giant ボス card, arguing about how to beat it. At the edge of the table, the small card with the folded paper cat sits untouched, its plain katakana facing up and unread.

exitImage.description: The giant ボス card is set aside, face down. In the middle of the table sits the small card reading ネコ, face up, the folded paper cat resting on top of it. On the game box, the little dog sticker captioned チェスナットさん watches over the whole thing.

scenes.goal: Meet Sam through a warm invitation that branches into more options than anyone can answer, and reach the point where generosity has become paralysis.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: When an invitation has too many options, will adding one more make it answerable, or does it have to be narrowed to a single ask?
scenes.learnerNeed: A real invitation that must be collapsed from a sprawl of options into one clear time-and-activity ask.

intents: Warmly invite the whole class to a get-together, and to be inclusive, put every possible option on the table at once.
Notice, out loud, that the invitation has grown so branched that nobody can find a place to answer it.
Realize that narrowing to a single askable choice, rather than adding more options, is what makes the invitation answerable.
Try to help by adding still more options — drinks, dessert — making the invitation even less answerable.

openingImage.description: The cafe's corner table already has glasses and a jug set out, poured before anyone agreed to anything. A notepad waits in the middle under Sam's pen.

exitImage.description: The extra branches fold away, leaving a single card with a time slot and an activity slot. Only the phrasing chunk that went missing — the time range or the invitation ending — returns for another try; the chosen day and activity stay put.

propCues.description: The notepad fills with branching options — days, dishes, drinks, tennis-first-or-after — arrows crossing arrows. The poured drinks sit untouched, going flat. Nobody at the table answers.

scenes.goal: Let Sam issue the single clear invitation, hear a real answer, and honor a soft refusal without re-asking.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: When the one clear invitation gets a soft 'no,' will Sam add another option to change it, or accept the answer he asked for?
scenes.learnerNeed: A stance on how to help Sam receive a hedged refusal as a complete answer and keep the door open.

intents: Issue the one clear invitation aloud, once, with an easy, built-in way to decline.
Accept the soft refusal as a complete answer, write it on the card without adding options, and turn his attention back to the people already at the table.
Turn the single invitation into a warm, standing open door — one clear ask, come whoever's free — closing the evening without chasing anyone.
Warmly decline this one time with a hedged, indirect refusal that still clearly means no, and leave the relationship open.

openingImage.description: On the cleared notepad, one line remains: Saturday, from six, okonomiyaki. Every other branch has been set aside. The card can finally be answered.

exitImage.description: One clear invitation, one honored answer. The Saturday card stays out on the table for whoever's free; the flat drinks are cleared and fresh ones poured for the people who are here now.

title.ja: この幕から先はネタバレ禁止

scenes.goal: Meet Francis hosting a serial-discussion night for people at different points, and reach the moment where a verdict cannot be spoken without spoiling.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: When half the room hasn't reached the good part, can enthusiasm become something other than a verdict?
scenes.learnerNeed: A bounded past-tense impression handed off with a question that a person at any point in the serial can answer.

intents: Welcome everyone and set the one rule the night runs on: because people are at different points, only what has already aired, spoken about in the past tense.
Quietly take one bounded hosting task off Rie — cover the door and re-steep her tea — as care shown by doing, not by announcing.
Get carried away agreeing, start to blurt the reveal, catch himself mid-sentence, and land on a bounded past-tense impression of his own reaction instead.
Replace the ranking with his signature move: a floor-opening question about what people have already seen, that a person at any point can answer, welcoming split answers.
Declare a flat verdict — name the best episode and where 'it all comes together' — which itself points a giant arrow at where the reveal lives.

openingImage.description: A paper curtain is strung across the back of the cafe with a hand-lettered sign: NO SPOILERS BEYOND THIS CURTAIN. A small round plush sits on the sill like a guard. Along the front tables, seat-cards mark how far each person has watched — 3話, 5話, 最終話 — no two the same. A manga volume lies face-down by a half-eaten plate; the host's hoodie carries a faint kitchen smell.

exitImage.description: The paper curtain stays drawn across the back of the cafe. But now voices cross it in both directions — careful, past-tense, none of them carrying the thing behind it. The plush on the sill has not had to move.

propCues.description: By the counter, a cup of tea sits where Rie set it down an hour ago, a thin skin cooling on its surface. She is three tables away, restacking chairs and steering two latecomers to seats, and has not come back to it. Francis, mid-sentence, notices the cup before anyone else does.

Two slots are set out side by side: a past-tense impression slot and a floor-opening question slot. Only the slot that leaked toward the reveal returns for another try; the safe half the learner already landed stays put.

scenes.goal: Discover that a 'safe' euphemism draws more attention to the twist than the answer would, and settle on a question as the thing that opens the floor.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: If hiding the reveal only points at it harder, what actually opens a room full of people at different points?
scenes.learnerNeed: A stance on how to open the floor without pointing at the secret — a question, or a marked opinion handed off with one.

intents: Try to stay safe by swapping the reveal for total euphemism — and accidentally make the whole room lean in harder, because the blur announces that a secret exists right there.
Take the point but keep his competitive shape — reframe his verdict as a challenge-question that is spoiler-safe, and name a friendly count-up later instead of ranking now.
Name why the euphemism fails — it plants an arrow that a secret exists right there — and why a single question opens the floor without pointing, leaving nobody behind even when answers split.
Close on his signature move — answer his own floor-opening question in bounded past tense, then turn it back to the room: that's where I'm at, where are you?

openingImage.description: Someone has taped a SAFE WORDS list to the wall: gentle stand-ins for the reveal — 「例の人」, 「例のこと」, 「アレ」. Under the curtain, the three seat-cards still mark three different stopping points. The list looks careful. It also looks like a treasure map.

exitImage.description: A phone buzzes face-up on the table — a shift reminder lights the screen. Francis glances at it, turns it face-down without reading past the first line, and looks back up at the room. Along the wall the seat-cards begin to move: everyone marking where they are, no two the same, and not one of them saying what's behind the curtain.

scenes.goal: Decode a pictureless hand-brushed ramen menu by kanji components, and reach the point where knowing what a dish is does not tell you what a person wants.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: When the expert can read every character, is that enough to order for someone else?
scenes.learnerNeed: A kanji-decoding and preference-ordering task where reading the menu only becomes useful once it meets someone's likes and a dietary limit.

intents: Wave off the panic at a picture-free wall menu and start reading it aloud, with the running joke that the characters are easy.
Crack one scary character into a memory image aloud, flag openly that it may be nonsense rather than the real origin, and land that it is now unforgettable.
Read the easy shape-and-meaning characters with certainty, then openly hedge on a reading he is only half-sure of, keeping the meaning and the reading honestly separate.
Name the honest limit of his expertise — he can decode what each dish is, but not what a person likes — and hand the preference choice back to the diner while pointing out the meat-free rows.
Turn the reading from a performance into a real problem by naming his own limit: he cannot eat meat and needs to know which bowl is safe.

openingImage.description: A cramped ramen counter before class. The whole wall is a hand-brushed menu: black characters on cream paper, no photos, no prices in numerals anyone can find fast. Steam curls up past the last empty stools.

exitImage.description: The wall menu no longer reads as a solid block. The 肉 dishes sit in one column, the 魚 and 野菜 dishes in another, and the meat-free bowl the learner picked out is circled in chalk. The steam behind the counter thickens as an order is called back.

propCues.description: One dish name lifts off the wall and splits into its left and right parts, side by side. Only the piece that went unread returns for another try; the parts already decoded stay in place, and the counter phrase waits underneath.

scenes.goal: Let Shin hand over the method rather than the answer, so his decoding becomes a shared tool and each person's likes decide their own bowl.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Can an expert's skill be more useful handed over than performed?
scenes.learnerNeed: A stance choice about how to use Shin's decoding method — take the answer, or take the route.

intents: Deliberately withhold the answer and offer the route instead — left half, right half — inviting the learner to decode the last character themselves.
Close on his own theme: the character is the easy part, even a made-up memory sticks, but what a person likes is the one thing only they can decide — and that is the hard part.
Place his own order for the meat-free bowl with a counter, warm and relieved to be able to ask for it plainly.

openingImage.description: Everyone has claimed a stool along the counter. One dish name near the bottom of the wall is still unread, and Shin taps it with the end of his pencil instead of saying it.

exitImage.description: Bowls land along the counter, one to each stool. Robert's meat-free bowl sits among them, no different to look at. Behind the diners the wall menu stays legible now — two columns, one circled line — the way Shin left it.

scenes.goal: Meet Jodi through her Tokyo photo and reach the point where one caption cannot hold a place that is half-there and half-gone.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: When a place is both remembered and changed, will the class force one true caption or keep two?
scenes.learnerNeed: A two-tense captioning task where saying it was X and is now Y, with one reason, matters more than choosing a single truth.

intents: Drop the wistful aside about having lived in Tokyo, show the corner, and say she wants to caption this street, opening with the past.
Accept the material fact, state that she can still recall it clearly because she lived here, and decide to write both tenses instead of choosing one.
Read both captions aloud, name both as true, and make clear she is deleting neither.
Ground the material fact from the concrete: she knows this corner, half of it still stands, but the bakery is gone and is a convenience store now, so one caption will not hold.

openingImage.description: A stack of old photographs goes hand to hand around the table for captioning. One stops in front of the class: a Tokyo street corner, a small shopfront on the left, the print soft at the edges. A blank caption slip waits beneath it.

exitImage.description: The photo now carries two caption slips at once — one in the past tense, one in the present — pinned side by side. Neither is crossed out. The corner in the picture stays exactly as half-there as it always was.

propCues.description: The past slip and the present slip are set side by side beneath the photo. Only the tense or the reason that went missing returns for another try; the caption already written stays in place, uncrossed.

scenes.goal: Let Jodi name why she keeps both tenses, and let the class treat plural memory as a form to master rather than a contradiction to fix.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Can two true sentences about one place count as finished, without one being made to win?
scenes.learnerNeed: A stance choice about how to hold two captions of one place open at once.

intents: Report her own past thought about the place with a quoted thought, and set both the losing and the keeping side by side as true.
Keep both captions and place one remembered detail in the past line and one visible detail in the present line.
Make a practical adjustment so both captions and the route beneath them remain readable.

openingImage.description: The photo rests under the desk lamp with both captions kept. Jodi looks at it for a moment longer than the task needs, the way you look at a place rather than a picture.

exitImage.description: The photo is pinned to the working atlas with both captions beneath it, shifted just far enough that the route line remains visible. Bread smell belongs to the past slip; the convenience-store light belongs to the present one. Neither is crossed out.

scenes.goal: Meet Christian through his complete card-by-card lantern procedure and hit the moment the wind takes the sequence apart.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: When the order blows away, will Christian rebuild a bigger system or let the steps be re-sequenced by the room?
scenes.learnerNeed: A live re-sequencing where putting te-form steps back in order with a reason matters more than owning the whole procedure.

intents: Welcome the learner and lay out his complete ordered card-by-card procedure for running the lantern's cloud.
Instead of simply restoring order, reach for a bigger system — more cards, larger numbers, the fan, a rota — and offer to own the whole fix.
Watch the cloud light in sequence and laugh at himself: the steps were right all along, only the order was missing — and he over-builds by reflex.
Redirect from enlarging the system to restoring the sequence: the steps are all correct, only the order was lost, so re-lay them one at a time with a reason instead of building more.

openingImage.description: In the courtyard, a brass weather-lantern sits on a bench. Beside it a stack of numbered instruction cards is pinned in order under a small clip; an electric desk fan hums at the end of the bench, and a phone glows nearby with a homework tab already open.

exitImage.description: The cloud runs its parts in sequence, one glow after another. One last card is still in Christian's hand, not yet pinned; he turns it over but does not add it to the row.

propCues.description: A gust crosses the courtyard and lifts the clip. The cards spin down shuffled, their numbers no longer in a row. On the lantern, every part of the cloud lights at once — a flat white glare instead of a sequence.
The re-laid cards stay where the learner placed them. Only the one card that landed out of sequence lifts back out for another try, its reason line shown blank beside it.

scenes.goal: Let Christian hand the last step to the room instead of pinning it himself, so the instruction guides without him owning it.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Can Christian let a step belong to everyone by giving its order and reason rather than his hands?
scenes.learnerNeed: A stance choice about how to make an instruction hand-off-able through sequenced request and cause.

intents: Pass the final card to the room with its order and reason, then take one bounded job instead of running the whole sequence.
Receive the handoff, add the reason to the card, and assign the next concrete jobs around the lantern.

openingImage.description: Christian sits on the bench with the last card still in his hand. The fan hums beside him; a small recorder is out on the bench too, and nobody says anything about it. He looks from the card to the people around the lantern.

exitImage.description: The cloud runs its whole sequence, one glow after another, with Christian's hands off it. The last card passes from person to person around the lantern. The fan hums on the bench; the recorder is still there, unremarked.

scenes.goal: Meet Alex on the sign-stripped street and rebuild the route he walked, in order.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: When the signs are gone, is a re-route a crisis or just the next set of steps?
scenes.learnerNeed: A te-form sequence of directions with place particles, recovered under changed conditions.

intents: Deliver the biggest fact of the night — every sign is gone — in the flattest possible voice.
Narrate a past travel experience to frame a lost route as a solvable inconvenience, not a crisis.
State how he reached the street as an ordered te-form sequence, ending on the calm clause 'long, but quiet'.
Confirm the learner's sequence flatly, treating a rebuilt route as unremarkable rather than a rescue.

openingImage.description: The exhibition street after the storm: every signpost stands bare, its route plate torn away. Puddles hold the last of the wind. One figure walks up without hurrying, a folded paper map in his coat pocket.

exitImage.description: A thin route line joins the rebuilt steps along the street — and runs straight into a corner where standing water fills the underpass. The line stops at the water's edge.

propCues.description: The steps already placed stay pinned along the street. Only the one connector that slipped out of order returns for another attempt.

scenes.goal: Let Aakash supply the back way around the flooded corner and let Alex change course without apology.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Can a plan change out loud, mid-route, and be stated as a decision rather than a failure?
scenes.learnerNeed: A stance on how to back a route that just changed — confirm the new sequence, or trust the flat report.

intents: Supply the commuter back way calmly — the classmate who once needed a route now hands one over, with place particles and clear turns.
Land the back way with easy warmth, offering the route as something to keep rather than a one-time rescue.
State the reroute as a settled plan with kotoninarimashita, and frame changing course as reason-giving, not apology.
Close on the calmest clause of all — a quiet, unstressed foreshadow that he is used to changing course and being away.

openingImage.description: The rebuilt route ends at the flooded underpass. Water sits across the whole corner. A second figure comes up the street from the far side, already gesturing past the water toward a narrow side lane.

exitImage.description: The route line redraws itself: it turns at the bakery, runs down the side lane, and ends at a lit doorway. The old flooded corner is simply left off the map, no longer a problem to solve.

scenes.goal: Watch Jenny's fully planned serving order vanish and see her ask the class into the scene instead of rescuing it alone.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: When every serving cue is gone, will the host keep carrying it alone or ask the room to count what is really there?
scenes.learnerNeed: A failed service plan where describing what remains and counting how many are needed rebuilds one course from the table itself.

intents: Welcome the class to a meal for the atlas's first route and lay out the serving plan she prepared in advance.
After trying privately to re-thread the plan alone, stop soldiering on and ask the class into the scene: describe what is still present and count how many are needed.
Answer the ask straight away by already having the table fed: the handout is photographed and shared, and he counts aloud what is present and still warm.

openingImage.description: The cafe counter is lined with covered dishes and a row of small serving cards, each meant to say what the dish is, how many there are, and when it goes out. Above the counter the class's paper atlas waits with one unlit route point at its edge.

exitImage.description: Plated to the count the room agreed on, one warm course is ready to go round. Above the counter, the single route point at the atlas's edge begins, faintly, to glow. Every other route stays blank.

propCues.description: One by one the serving cards go blank — every label, every count, every order-arrow wiped away. Jenny, a half-finished scarf still looped over one wrist, coaxes one tangled serving-string back into place, then looks up at the covered dishes waiting without a single label.
One covered dish is set forward on its own beside an empty count-slot. Only the single item that went uncounted returns for another try; the parts already described and counted stay in place.

scenes.goal: Let the first ensemble save land as one restored short route, and let Jenny name it as enough without claiming the whole atlas is back.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Can restoring one course together count as a real win while the map is still unfinished?
scenes.learnerNeed: A stance choice for how to back a recovery the class made together, using an offer or a counted request.

intents: Notice the one route and ask the room what to send next, leaving the shared recovery visible in the dish that made it around the table.

openingImage.description: The one warm course leaves the counter and starts round the table. On the atlas the single lit route point holds steady while the rest of the map stays dark. Jenny watches it move, the half-finished scarf resting now against her arm.

exitImage.description: The one course has gone all the way round the table. The single lit route holds on the atlas; the rest of the map is still blank. The serving cards now lie within everyone's reach. In Jenny's lap, one stitch returns to the half-finished scarf.

scenes.goal: Meet Robert through his over-planned dinner sequence and hit the one condition it cannot hold.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: When the plan breaks, will the host add more options or hear what is actually needed?
scenes.learnerNeed: A changed-plan negotiation where comparing two options matters more than completing a chain.

intents: Welcome the class broadly, then lay out the full if-then dinner order he prepared.
Under pressure, cover the gap by piling on more options instead of stopping.
After watching quietly, make one precise request that trades the broken chain for a real choice.

openingImage.description: The cafe's long table is set not with food but with ordered cards: soup, salad, pasta, each pinned to the next with a hand-drawn arrow. Steam waits behind the counter.

exitImage.description: Robert takes down the extra cards. One dish remains on the table, with no arrow after it. The gap is simply left.

propCues.description: A delivery crate is short one box. The card that says 'salad' no longer has anything behind its arrow. The chain now points at nothing.
The two remaining cards are set side by side. Only the comparison phrase that went missing returns for another try; the earlier decision stays.

scenes.goal: Let Robert redesign the evening around what he heard instead of what he planned.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Can a host count leaving a gap as good hosting?
scenes.learnerNeed: A stance choice about how to back a plan that has been made smaller on purpose.

intents: Accept the smaller plan out loud, and reframe hosting as listening rather than covering every gap.

openingImage.description: For the first time all evening Robert sits down instead of moving between cards. He turns the one remaining card face up and leaves it.

exitImage.description: One dish goes round the table and is enough. The empty arrow-space stays on the card, no longer a problem to solve.

scenes.goal: Meet Sophie mid-argument over one contested particle and reach the point where grammar alone cannot decide.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: When two particles are both correct, will the class vote one into truth or test each against its context?
scenes.learnerNeed: A changed-context trial where explaining why two readings hold matters more than picking the single right answer.

intents: Name the two candidate particles and the distinction precisely, then lean toward closing the case with に as the clean answer.
Stop trying to declare a winner and instead propose building, one at a time, the context in which each particle is correct.
Accept that both particles are correct in different contexts, mark her confidence honestly, and record the number together with the context of each rather than choosing one.
Bring a concrete counted observation that fits で just as well, so grammar alone can no longer pick the answer.

openingImage.description: On the rebuilt map, one route caption reads 「この灯りは一時間◯三回つきます」 with the particle slot left open. Two classmates have penciled different answers over it: に and で. Neither has been erased.

exitImage.description: Sophie leaves the caption's particle slot open and lays a small notebook beside the map. On its first page the number three is written twice — once under a per-hour card, once under a one-observed-hour card.

propCues.description: The two contexts are set out side by side: a per-hour rhythm card and a single-observed-hour card. Only the context that went unmatched returns for another try; the matched one stays put.

scenes.goal: Let the class start a record that keeps two correct answers with their contexts instead of publishing one verdict.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Can a notebook count as more precise for holding two answers than a caption that shows one?
scenes.learnerNeed: A stance choice about whether a record should display an answer or preserve evidence with its context.

intents: Frame the notebook as a record of what was checked and its context, not a place to display the correct answer.
Reframe precision as keeping two conditioned readings rather than collapsing to one, and name it as the class's practice going forward.
Leave the caption's gap open on purpose and point it to the notebook, closing the evening without a single-answer verdict.
Widen from the single caption to the long view: this is how the atlas can hold several memories at once instead of one overwritten truth.

openingImage.description: The small notebook lies open between Sophie and Rose. It is ruled into two columns: one headed for a claim, one headed for the context it was counted in. Sophie uncaps a blue pen and a green one; the claim column is still empty.

exitImage.description: The caption keeps its open slot with a small mark pointing off the page. Beside the map the notebook stays open, the number three recorded twice in blue and green, each under its own context. Nothing is crossed out.

scenes.goal: Meet Xingyu's flawed study chorus and locate the one dropped beat that makes it stick.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: When a chant is catchy because it is broken, will the room repair the sound or roast the flaw?
scenes.learnerNeed: A listening repair where catching one dropped katakana matters more than counting the beat.

intents: Offer the catchy but flawed chant openly, name the hole, and ask for a repair while asking plainly not to be mocked.
Hand the repair to the learner: sing it once more and ask for the missing katakana by ear, one letter.
Escalate the offer into a contest and sing the gap back with relish, tipping the flaw toward a bit.
Count the beats to locate the hole exactly, then mark that the count proves where, not which sound.

openingImage.description: Three katakana cards are taped across the board in a row: ライト, ルート, and a third whose middle is left blank. Xingyu taps the desk in time and hums a tune that stumbles on a small gap right at the third card.

exitImage.description: The third card now reads full, and Xingyu taps four beats where he had been tapping three. The tune keeps its bounce; only the stumble is gone.

propCues.description: Half the room is already humming it back — and everyone hums the gap too, landing on the same little silence where the beat should be. The flaw is the part that stuck.
The third card is held up with its blank still open, and Xingyu sings only the short word again, slower. Just the one dropped sound waits for another try; the rest of the chant stays as it was.

scenes.goal: Let the repaired chant stay Xingyu's, with the flaw received kindly instead of roasted.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Can the room fix the sound without laughing the fun out of the offer?
scenes.learnerNeed: A casual reaction that backs an imperfect thing offered aloud without turning it into a target.

intents: Drop the winner-take-all framing and redesign the game so the old hole is a clap everyone shares and nobody loses.
Accept the shared clap: fix the sound but keep the pause on purpose, and say plainly that putting the flawed thing out there was worth it.
Mark the kept pause as the beat the whole room now lands on together, treating the timing as the thing that holds it.

openingImage.description: Xingyu hums the whole chant through once, clean now. Tom is up on the balls of his feet, plainly itching to turn it into a contest again.

exitImage.description: The room runs the chant once through: three full words, and on the fourth beat that used to be a hole, everyone claps together. The gap is kept on purpose now.

title.en: The Night the Map Went Dark

scenes.goal: Meet Angel through a perfectly documented fix, then watch the exactly-correct instruction erase the visible route.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: When the only copy of the route is the light, does a correct command make the room safer or leave it stranded?
scenes.learnerNeed: A cause-and-technology beat where a literally-right instruction produces the failure and the class must decide how to hold the knowledge.

intents: Enter by converting the flicker into a documented, step-ordered fix that the card guarantees will work.
Stop Rie and expose the assumption in the plan: the command was not wrong, and that is exactly why it erased the display.
Under the blackout, narrow to procedure and take the whole recovery onto herself so no one else has to work.

openingImage.description: The rebuilt route glows across the wall, flickering at one corner. The paper map on the table beneath it is blank; the light is the only copy. Angel stands at the console with a printed step-card, checking it line by line.

exitImage.description: No one is looking at the wall anymore. Chairs shift away from the dark projection and into a loose circle. The blank paper map is passed to the middle.

propCues.description: The reset runs exactly as written. The flicker stops — and so does everything else. The route, every label, drains off the wall. The paper underneath stays blank. The room's only copy of the map was the light.

scenes.goal: Preserve the erased route by teaching it back — each person explaining a segment and its cause — while Rie accepts one bounded job instead of all of them.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Can a route that lived only on the screen survive by living in the people who remember it?
scenes.learnerNeed: A teach-back transfer: explain a cause with te-form, teach one segment back, compare the old display route with the new one, and state an opinion.

intents: Turn the loss into a method: the route is not gone because people hold it; each explains a segment and its cause, and it goes onto paper instead of the screen.
Offer Rie one specific bounded job — checking the joins at the end — and give the segments to the class, with an easy way to keep or decline it.
Reflexively reach back for the whole task, reluctant to make everyone else work.
Accept the one bounded job and hand the segments to the class instead of doing everything herself.
Expose the assumption in the original plan and change it: a correct command is not enough; the next card will document what a command erases, for the people who use it.

openingImage.description: The wall stays dark. No one is at the console. Henry sits in the circle with the blank paper map and a pen — not the keyboard — turning it so everyone can reach it.

exitImage.description: The route comes back across the blank paper map, drawn from spoken pieces in several different hands. The wall stays dark. The class is holding the map now, not the screen; Rie signs off only the seams.

propCues.description: The segments already taught back stay on the paper. Only the one cause-and-segment that did not land clearly returns for another try; the joins Rie is watching hold.

scenes.goal: Meet Felix through the way he tracks the paper-cat marker, and let his delight expose that the route cards are mislabeled.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Can watching a marker for fun do the work that the printed labels cannot?
scenes.learnerNeed: A way to identify which card is which by describing where the cat sits, not by reading a label that is wrong.

intents: Notice with delight that the single paper cat has moved to a different card than yesterday, and get the class to look.
Turn the delight into a method: propose tracing only the card the cat is on, count the cards and the cat, and pass the question to the room.
State a direct preference: read how the cards actually sit over what the wrong numbers claim, and back the card the cat is on.

openingImage.description: The library's reading table holds five route cards in a row, each stamped with a printed number. A small folded paper cat sits on one of them, facing the others. The numbers do not run left to right.

exitImage.description: One by one the cards are drawn into the sequence the cat has been sitting through. The printed numbers stay stamped where they are, ignored. A thin trail is now visible in the placement itself.

propCues.description: Someone turns the cards to read the stamped numbers aloud: two, then five, then one. The printed order contradicts itself, and no card can be trusted by its own label. The class stalls over which card really comes first.
The marked card is lifted a little clear of the row so only it and the cat are in view. Just the relative-clause phrasing that slipped returns for another attempt; the count of cards stays as it was.

scenes.goal: Let the class settle the real card order using the cat's trail, and let Felix name joy as a way of working rather than a distraction from it.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Does an observation that began as play count as evidence the class can build on?
scenes.learnerNeed: A stance on whether to declare the cat's trail as the order outright or verify it card by card first.

intents: Accept that the trail he followed for fun matched the real order, and reframe delight as a way of paying attention rather than a distraction from work.

openingImage.description: Felix lines up where the cat has sat on each past evening. The marks fall into one unbroken line across the cards — a walkway the cat has been pacing while the labels stayed wrong. He stops moving and just looks at it.

exitImage.description: The class reads the five cards aloud in the cat's order and the route holds. The paper cat is set on the last card in the line, facing the empty table, ready to move again the next evening.

title.ja: 記おくカードびじゅつかん

scenes.goal: Meet Stasi through her card museum and her funniest card, and hit the moment the joke turns out to name the wrong component.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Can the class correct a memorable card without turning it into a plain one?
scenes.learnerNeed: A revision task where component evidence has to change a kanji claim while the vivid picture is protected.

intents: Welcome the class to her card museum, show off her favorite card's vivid mouth-and-tree picture, and say she wants to turn the whole wall into a flashcard program.
Accept the correction reluctantly, and name the real worry: that the accurate version will lose what made the card memorable.
Turn the wall into a fast speed round, race to name the parts, and confidently blurt the wrong component before moving on.
Stop the race, decompose the character by its actual strokes, and show the part is 未 (not 木) — carrying both a meaning and the reading.

openingImage.description: The classroom's side board has become a small museum: rows of hand-drawn kanji memory cards pinned in a grid, each with its own picture. In front of one card — 味, drawn as a wide-open mouth clamped over a leafy branch — a small knot of people has gathered. The projector shows an empty flashcard shell, waiting to be filled.

exitImage.description: Only the sentence about the button and the changed part returns for another pass. The picture and the earlier welcome stay exactly where they were.

propCues.description: On the projector the two shapes sit side by side, 木 and 未, with the extra top stroke of 未 circled. Below them the empty program shell now shows a single labelled control: a part button marked ぶひん, waiting for what it should reveal.

scenes.goal: Let Stasi rebuild her card so it stays vivid and becomes accurate, and let Tom's speed cost land as a redesigned game rather than a scolding.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Can accuracy and expression share the same card, and can a fast challenge hold both?
scenes.learnerNeed: A stance choice about how to back a corrected card and a challenge that outran itself.

intents: Take the correction and rebuild the card in her own vivid style — dropping the tree, keeping the mouth, and making 未 into a picture of tasting something not yet ripe.
Close the beat by claiming both at once: the first museum piece is funny and true, and both can stand together.
Own that his speed produced the wrong answer, and redesign the challenge so accuracy comes before the race instead of dropping the game.
Confirm briefly that the revised card holds up on both the parts and the sound, and is still hard to forget.

openingImage.description: On the projector the revised card draft has appeared: the same wide-open mouth, but now clamped over a hard green fruit, with 未 labelled beside it and the ぶひん button sitting underneath, ready to press.

exitImage.description: The revised card goes back on the wall as the museum's first finished piece — the mouth still mid-bite, 未 in the corner, the ぶひん button glowing on the projector beside it. The wrong stroke is gone; the joke is not.

scenes.goal: Watch a clip pitched above the class's comfort level and keep going after its subtitles fail.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: When the safety rail of full text disappears, does the class stop, or read what it can?
scenes.learnerNeed: A way to state a person's intent from an incomplete source while keeping heard and inferred parts separate.

intents: Bring a clip she knows is above the class's level and frame an ordinary breakfast shot as a scene worth the reach.
Instead of stopping, keep the class watching by reading the scene off tone and faces, and offer that most of it can still be followed.
Agree to continue, but require that what was actually heard stay marked apart from what is being inferred, so partial comprehension remains checkable.

openingImage.description: The library's back corner is dark except for a paused frame on the wall screen: a kitchen, a bowl, a person half-turned toward a window. A subtitle line sits ready under it. Ruparna stands beside the screen, not the switch.

exitImage.description: Two columns stand on the whiteboard: one of lines the class actually caught, one of what it read in. Neither column pretends to be the other. The blank subtitle bar still glows under the paused frame.

propCues.description: The clip starts. The subtitle line stutters into broken glyphs, then goes blank and stays blank. The picture and the voices keep running with nothing written under them. Two people near the front shift in their seats.

Only the one moment that stayed unclear is scrubbed back and played again, a little slower. The heard-and-inferred columns already filled in stay on the whiteboard; just the ambiguous line waits for another read.

scenes.goal: Count the partial comprehension honestly and decide whether about seventy percent is enough to continue.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Is readiness a switch that is on or off, or a door that opens partway?
scenes.learnerNeed: A stance on continuing from partial comprehension without either overclaiming or refusing to move.

intents: Tally what actually held up, put a number on it — about seventy percent — and frame the missing thirty as unknown rather than failed.
Treat the certain seventy percent as enough for one next scene, leave the rest visibly unconfirmed, and keep the next viewing optional.

openingImage.description: The clip pauses on the last frame. Sophie caps the marker and steps back so the two columns are both readable. The heard column is longer than the seats near the front expected.

exitImage.description: The blank subtitle bar stays blank under the last frame. A small tag beside it reads 'unconfirmed'. Under the tag, Ruparna writes one short note: 「次の場面へ」.

scenes.goal: Rebuild the lost route from what people remember, and hit the moment where the accounts refuse to agree.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: When the memories diverge, does the class restore one true copy or keep them plural?
scenes.learnerNeed: A record-building task where preparing in advance and comparing accounts matters more than choosing a single winner.

intents: Notice the physical evidence first, then widen to the human problem: everyone remembers the route a little differently, and forcing one copy would lose that.
Stop the erasing and propose preparing a record in advance that holds all three, counted side by side, without voting one into truth.
Lay out his remembered route as a flat sequence, understated like a timetable, without insisting it is the only true one.
Hold her remembered route against what the card says now, layering two times without resolving which is correct.

openingImage.description: The atlas backing panel lies flat on the long classroom table, its old pencil route half rubbed away. Three blank index cards wait along it. Rose crouches to table height, reading the paper's wear before anyone's writing.

exitImage.description: The three cards sit in a numbered row along the backing, each route intact. The hovering eraser is capped and set down. The old fold-crease still shows underneath them all.

propCues.description: Three cards now sit along the backing, each tracing the same stretch a different way. A pencil eraser hovers over two of them, ready to make the map agree with itself.
The two diverging cards are set square against Alex's sequence. Only the comparison phrase that slipped comes back for another pass; the accounts already counted stay where they are.

scenes.goal: Fit three counted accounts onto a label that seems built for a single line.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Can one exhibition label hold a memory that stays plural?
scenes.learnerNeed: A stance choice about how to keep several accounts visible when the display asks for one.

intents: Point out, understated, that the exhibition label only has room for one line, so it looks like a single account will have to be chosen.
Read the finalized record back as a clean sequence that now carries the plural stretch, saying just enough and no more.
Layer the plan by adding attribution across time: note whose memory and from when beside each account so none is absorbed into another.
Read what the worn paper actually supports, then keep the disputed stretch plural because the material cannot choose among the accounts.

openingImage.description: The backing stands upright now, the three cards clipped along the route line. A printed exhibition label waits beside it with one narrow slot marked 'the route'.

exitImage.description: The finished label carries the shared stretch as one line and the diverging stretch marked as remembered several ways. Three faint routes stay on the backing, counted, none erased, the old fold-crease still visible beneath them.

scenes.goal: Meet Peter as he turns a stalled single-memory recital into one strong question per learner, and rebuild the first dark block by teach-back.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: When one memory runs out, does the district need a better memory, or a better question?
scenes.learnerNeed: A build-and-carry attempt where forming one precise question and repeating the answer back matters more than knowing the whole area.

intents: Name the one small detail he is certain of, admit he does not hold the whole district, and say he wants the dark area back.
Before the room gives up, ask one framing question that trades one whole memory for one piece from each person.
Invite the learner, with an easy way to decline, to build the next question themselves: pick one classmate, ask one clear thing, then repeat the answer back for the class to pin.
Confirm that one block came back, and name that the question, not one big memory, did the work.

openingImage.description: One district of the projected classroom map has gone dark. The cards pinned along it are blank, and the class has crowded around a single chair, waiting for the one person who might remember the whole area. Peter sits apart at the edge of the room, watching.

exitImage.description: One block of the map warms back to light. The card that was blank now carries a single line in the learner's hand. The rest of the district stays dark — but the chair in the middle is empty now; no one is waiting for a perfect memory anymore.

propCues.description: Someone takes the single chair and tries to recite the whole district from memory, shop by shop. Three shops in, the list runs dry. The blank cards stay blank. The room keeps its eyes on the chair, waiting for a better memory to arrive.
Only the question comes back for another pass — the classmate and their one remembered detail stay in place. The half-formed question is set down and picked up again, one word at a time.

scenes.goal: Spread the one-question-each method across the rest of the dark district, and let Peter's watching turn into leading.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Can a method the class runs itself be led by the person who only asks questions?
scenes.learnerNeed: A stance choice about how to carry a working method forward without one person owning the district.

intents: Decline to take the whole thing over; name that the same one-question move works again, and hand it back to the room with an open question.
Forecast that at this rate the whole district returns tonight, and name his role as watching-turned-leading: he sees where questions stall and hands the next one across.
Volunteer to go next by turning his own one remembered detail into a question and passing it to whoever would know the block beyond it — making question-passing the method.
Report gladly and briefly that the passed question pulled the next block back into the light.

openingImage.description: Half the district is lit now, block by block, each card in a different hand. The class has stopped looking at the single chair and started looking at Peter, who has not moved from the edge of the room.

exitImage.description: Card by card, the district comes back to light, each in a different hand. Peter stays at the edge where he began, but now the questions move out from him and the answers come back to the room. The single empty chair in the middle stays empty. No one sits in it.

title.en: The Blank Space on the Board

scenes.goal: Play the rebuilt route as a fast speaking game and hit the point where its polite lines jam under the clock.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: When a formal line stalls under time, will the class add more polish or change the register?
scenes.learnerNeed: A register shift that reopens a stalled exchange when the wording, not the meaning, is what broke.

intents: Turn the rebuilt route dialogue into a timed speaking game so visitors will actually talk instead of read the cards.
Seize the observation as a game move and dare the learner to flip the stalled line live — reopen the exchange casually, then land the reply polite, inside the timer.
Confirm the flipped line runs inside the timer and the game finally flows, and credit Shaun's register read without ceremony.
Enter late with a light, self-deprecating remark and take up as little space as possible.
Make one bounded observation that the stalled line is in written-notice register where a fast game needs casual speech, offered as an option and easy to ignore.

openingImage.description: The classroom board carries the rebuilt route as a row of dialogue cards, each pinned in order. A five-second game timer sits under them. One card near the middle is still blank, its slot unfilled.

exitImage.description: The card that stood blank now holds two lines — one casual, one polite — with a small arrow between them. The other route cards stay in their formal register, unchanged. The game timer resets to zero.

propCues.description: A player reaches the keigo card and runs out of sentence before the timer runs out; the buzzer cuts in. As it does the door opens and Shaun slips in late, setting a flattened paper bag on the side table. The blank card is still blank.

The single blank card is split down the middle: the casual opening on one side, the polite reply on the other. Only the register that slipped is offered again; the choice of which line goes where stays.

scenes.goal: Fold the late arrival's register read into the game without turning it into a role he did not ask for.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Can a bounded contribution count without being enlarged into a job?
scenes.learnerNeed: A stance choice about how much to hand a person who offered exactly one small thing.

intents: Offer one small, bounded thing — call out when a line's register turns stiff during the round — and make it easy to wave away.
Accept the small part as small, decline any enlargement, and stay light without explaining himself.
Design the next round so the casual/polite toggle is the game itself, and write Shaun's call-out into the rules as a fair signal rather than a spotlight.

openingImage.description: The board now shows each route beat in two columns — casual and polite — with the once-blank card at the head of the row. Shaun stays near the door, the flattened pastry unwrapped on a napkin, watching the next round set up.

exitImage.description: The next round starts with each card offering two registers and a small marker beside the once-blank slot for Shaun's signal. He stays by the door, calling out only when a line turns stiff. The blank space on the board is gone, filled not by one right answer but by a register chosen out loud each time.

scenes.goal: Meet Nanako on the last evening of her London visit and watch the ordered farewell plan meet a clock it cannot beat.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: When the plan will not fit, does the group force the order or change what has to happen first?
scenes.learnerNeed: A changed-plan production where stating a revised intention and its before/after order matters more than keeping the original sequence.

intents: Tell the group this is the last time she can see them on this visit, and lay out the ordered thing she had meant to do before leaving: cook one dish together, eat, then thank each of them.
Accept that the dish itself may not get made, note that the thanks work without it, and hand the exact new order to the group to state.
Accept the revised sequence the learner set, and say plainly that if the cooking never happens, that is all right too.
Make one bounded suggestion that trades the broken order for a workable one: if the cooking will not fit, put it last and do the thank-yous first.

openingImage.description: A hand-drawn timeline runs across the cafe board: 作る → 食べる → お礼. Beside it hangs a clock. The kitchen behind the counter is still busy with someone else's order; the first step has not begun, and the last step is the one the group circled twice.

exitImage.description: The board now reads お礼 first; 作る sits behind a small 「時間があれば」. The stove stays cold. Behind the counter, someone lays out a row of name cards for the thank-you round instead of plates.

propCues.description: The counter is not free yet, and the clock leaves less time than the three steps need. On the board the 作る arrow still points at an empty stove. The order that was meant to end in thanks now cannot even start.
The board is wiped to just two boxes, お礼 and 作る. Only the before/after word between them returns for another try; the decision to put thanks first stays.

scenes.goal: Run the reordered thank-you round and let it not finish, so the group decides what to do with the words that go unsaid.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Can a farewell count the half-said thanks as enough, or must every word be forced out before she goes?
scenes.learnerNeed: A stance choice about unfinished gratitude: compress it into one line now, or leave it deliberately unfinished and held over.

intents: Take the first turn herself and thank the group for keeping a place for her whenever she returns to London.
Accept the half-finished round without asking for the missing lines, and reframe the unsaid thanks as something kept for a next meeting rather than lost.
Leave on a sentence she does not finish, keeping the rest available for a next meeting without promising when it must happen.
Name plainly that the round will not reach everyone, without proposing to fix it, so the choice about the unsaid thanks is on the table.

openingImage.description: The name cards lie in a row, one per friend at the table, each meant for a single line of thanks. A few are turned face up and spoken; most are still face down. The clock has crept close to the time Nanako has to leave.

exitImage.description: The door closes. On the table the thank-you cards stay half turned, the spoken ones and the unspoken ones side by side. Nobody flips the rest over. The unfinished round is simply left, held over, not cleaned up.

propCues.description: At the counter a hand turns down the lamp over the table. The borrowed evening is nearly up. More than half the name cards are still face down when the room goes quiet, waiting on what the learner will do with the rest.
Nanako gathers her coat and stands by the door. The board still reads お礼 first, the stove still cold, the cards still half turned. Nothing has been cleared away.

scenes.goal: Reach the moment the class realizes the last route cannot be fixed with more machine, and reframe it as a voice the route is missing.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Ten minutes from opening, will the class add one more fix or change what kind of thing they are trying to do?
scenes.learnerNeed: A stance on a plan that stops adding options and commits to coordinating people instead.

intents: Join the shared call from a distance in the last ten minutes, greet quickly, and name the plain facts visible through the camera: the last route is dark and everyone is crowded at the machine.
Reframe the whole problem: it is not the machine — this route lights when people read it in time, so propose coordinating voices instead of adding hardware.
Welcome Mira into the call, then, under the clock, keep stacking conditional fixes onto the machine instead of stopping.
Hear it, set the cable down, and switch from adding options to lining people up — hosting becomes coordinating who reads what and when.

openingImage.description: The winter courtyard is strung for the exhibition. The lantern-atlas glows along every route but the last one, which stays black end to end. The class is packed around a projector cart at its base, feeding it cables. A phone propped against the cart has just connected to the shared call, its camera pointed at the dark route.

exitImage.description: The cables go slack on the ground and the cart is rolled to one side. Someone lifts the phone from it and props it beside the first route card. The class turns from the machine to the map, spreading into a loose line along the dark route.

propCues.description: The cable is swapped. A second projector hums on. The brightness dial goes up. The final route stays exactly as black as before. Behind the fence, the first guests begin to line up.

scenes.goal: Turn the reframed plan into a live coordinated narration that lights the final route, and let the success open the next season's question.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Can a class light a map by agreeing on conditions and keeping their voices in time with one another?
scenes.learnerNeed: An integrated production where the learner negotiates a conditional plan and calls a route live for a coordinated group.

intents: Lock the plan into three plain conditions, then hand the live calling to the learner with an easy way to decline.
Land the finale's relationship point lightly: she joined the call for the last ten minutes and it still changed the outcome, then prompt the people on site to open the doors.
Confirm the route lit, and name plainly that it answered coordinated timing rather than any new hardware or magic — the same mechanism as the very first evening, now carried by everyone together.

openingImage.description: Along the dark route, Stasi has laid the segment cards out in reading order, colour-edged so each hand-off is visible at a glance. Each person picks up the card in front of them. Mira's voice comes from the phone beside the first card. The route waits, unlit.

exitImage.description: As the finished route settles into a steady glow, one panel in the atlas backing catches the light from behind — a line of older handwriting the projection never threw onto the wall, with no name in the field beside it. Rose, gathering the spare cables at the back, stops with her hand flat against it.

propCues.description: Ruparna walks the route once, tracing it with a fingertip and setting a small chalk tick at each corner where a voice must breathe so the next one does not collide with it. The order is agreed; only the timing between voices is still loose.
The route holds up to the corner where two voices overlapped. Only that single hand-off is taken again on the same agreed order; the segments already lit stay lit while the learner re-times the pass.

scenes.goal: Meet the class the day after the exhibition arguing over what one polite parting phrase meant, and reach the point where hearing every word is not the same as knowing the intent.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: When a phrase is heard perfectly and still means three things, will the class vote one reading true or keep all three with their evidence?
scenes.learnerNeed: A way to name the several intents one polite phrase can carry while keeping the words and pause that were heard apart from the intent being inferred.

intents: Report the visitor's parting phrase in reported speech, mark his own read of it as praise as an opinion rather than a verdict, frame it as an ambiguous final panel, and open the floor.
Refuse to let Mika's read drop, name the pause itself as evidence and part of the same panel, and propose laying out each person's heard reading side by side instead of choosing one.
Offer his timing read — a long pause sat before the phrase, unlike a praising pause — then start to yield the floor by suggesting he might have misheard.
Hold his timing read as expertise instead of yielding it — cite the near-second pause as data — and ask that his reading be recorded as one of the three, not the loser of a vote.

openingImage.description: The classroom the day after the first exhibition. The booth banner lies folded over a desk. In the corner of the whiteboard, last term's small tag still hangs — 「聞こえた／未確認 — 約7割」. Ruparna, leaning by the door, taps it once and says nothing. Beneath it Francis has written a single line: 「……けっこうです」, the last thing one visitor said on the way out.

exitImage.description: Three readings now stand side by side on the board — 褒め, ためらい, お断り — each with the evidence that fed it: the words, the length of the pause, the fall of the voice. None is crossed out. The visitor's line stays written exactly as it was said.

propCues.description: Three blank reading-cards are set out — 褒め / ためらい / お断り. Only the reading that went untagged returns for another pass, its evidence line still empty; the readings already backed by the words, the pause, or the tone stay where they are.

scenes.goal: Decide how to write the feedback down so it keeps three intents and the speaker's own register instead of rounding into a clean compliment.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Should the record smooth the phrase into praise, or hold the visitor's exact words with their three possible intents kept apart?
scenes.learnerNeed: A stance on whether a record repairs only the listener's mishearing or rewrites the speaker's words, and how to keep register while separating said from meant.
