intents: Bring a register-reading ear from years of client email: the same phrase carries three implications, so copying the words alone is not enough — which implication it was said with has to be kept.

Set the boundary that turns editing into honesty: fix only the listeners' own mishearing, and leave the visitor's words in the visitor's register — tidying it into a clean compliment would be speaking in their place.

Agree through the ambiguous-panel frame and name the temptation — rounding the phrase into praise is easiest but makes the visitor say what they didn't — then open the question of how to record it honestly.
Close by tying the open record back to the class's seventy-percent principle — hearing all of it is not understanding all of it — and hand the floor back with his signature question.

openingImage.description: The three readings are still on the board. Peter has turned up in the seat by the side wall that nobody had thought to check, notebook already open. The visitor's line waits below, unrounded.

exitImage.description: The record now reads the phrase verbatim — 「……けっこうです」, pause and all — with three intents tagged beneath it as separate inferences. Beside it the old 約7割 tag has a line added: 全部聞こえても、全部は分からない. Nothing has been smoothed into a compliment; the visitor's words stay in the visitor's register.

title.ja: 持ち主のいないキャプション

scenes.goal: Reveal the ownerless caption Rose found under the atlas backing and reach the point where no reliable author can be recovered.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: When a found sentence has no author to name, does the class invent an owner to close the gap, or describe the gap as it is?
scenes.learnerNeed: A way to describe a found record — nominalizing what it says and marking its author as unknown — without inventing the source it does not have.

intents: Reveal the physically found caption by describing the material exactly — the different paper, the old ink, where it sat under the backing — and stop before its meaning or its maker.

State the exact limit of the material evidence — the paper and ink are provable, the author is not — and refuse to fill a name they do not have, the refusal that will force the plan to change rather than a technical fix.
Reach for a reliable author field — a signature, a date, a mark, some record of the maker — run the whole backing for it, and find nothing, the workaround reflex hitting a wall.

Accept that no author field will fix this, drop the shortcut, and redesign the record to state the absence honestly instead of inventing an owner — his late qualifier defending the impulse a beat before he changes the action.

openingImage.description: In the library, the exhibition atlas lies face-down on the worktable, its cloth backing peeled back at one corner. On the old paper underneath, a single caption is written in faded ink — a complete sentence — and above it, where a signature line would sit, there is nothing. Rose's fingers rest at the peeled corner. In the margin beside the caption, Shin has already penciled the reading over every character; the author line stays blank.

exitImage.description: The caption lies face-up with its author line still blank. Beside it, a description card now reads what the sentence is and that its writer is unknown — no name invented, no owner assigned. Shin's full reading sits in the margin, every character legible, the author still nobody.

propCues.description: Two description cards are set out side by side: one that assigns a maker — 『◯◯によって書かれた』 with the name space still empty — and one that nominalizes the content and states plainly that the author is unknown. Only the card that reached past the evidence into naming returns for another try; the honest description stays where it is.

scenes.goal: Start a record that keeps the caption with its source marked as absent, and widen from the one caption to how the whole atlas holds many hands.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Can 'the source is unknown' be recorded as a fact worth keeping, rather than a blank that must be filled?
scenes.learnerNeed: A stance on how a record should hold a found thing whose author cannot be recovered.

intents: Frame the record as holding two things — what the caption is and where it came from — with no name guessed, and name the absence itself as real information.

Reframe precision as marking exactly how far the evidence reaches and no further, using her farm register — the deliberately empty line is the accurate part — and set it as how the class reads found things from now on.

Widen slowly from the one caption to the whole atlas — it was never one person's; it holds many hands laid in over time, so 'whose is it' was the wrong question, and keeping the hands without erasing them is all it needs.

openingImage.description: On the worktable, the atlas backing lies open beside the described caption. A fresh record sheet is ruled with two headings: one for what the caption is, one for where it came from. The what-heading has the sentence under it already. The source line is still empty.

exitImage.description: The caption stays face-up, its author line blank on purpose. The record sheet reads what the sentence is and that its source is unknown — several hands, no name. Nothing is invented, nothing is crossed out. The atlas backing is laid flat again over its many layers.

propCues.description: Henry writes on the source line: the caption, and beside it 'source — unknown; passed through several hands, no name.' The what-line is full; the source line now carries a described absence rather than a guess. Nothing is entered where the author would be.

scenes.goal: Meet Sophie proud of a polished rewrite and reach the point where a correct fix has quietly erased the writer's voice.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: When an edit fixes the error but replaces the person, is it still a correction?
scenes.learnerNeed: A bounded rewrite where repairing the one real mistake matters, and keeping the writer's voice and stance matters more than making the sentence smoother.

intents: Present her polished rewrite as an improvement, noting she fixed one real verb-form error and smoothed the whole caption for the exhibition, and lean toward using her version.

Catch that she did two different things at once — repaired an error and replaced a voice — apologize for acting without asking, and propose keeping Peter's sentence while fixing only the single wrong spot.

Name the distinction cleanly and mark her confidence honestly: she was right about the one verb form, but whether the sentence is good enough for the exhibition was never hers to decide — that belongs to its writer. Repair the error, leave the voice.
Agree the fixed spot is correct, then name quietly that the rewrite no longer sounds like him — it sounds like nobody — because his closing question, the part he most wanted, is gone.
Confirm quietly that the caption reads like him again — corrected, not erased — with the closing question still standing, and thank her.

openingImage.description: Two caption cards sit side by side on the exhibition board. The left is Peter's own draft for a dark route point: 「この道は、だれも通らなくなってから、ずっと灯りがつけている。だれのためだろう。」 The right is Sophie's rewrite: 「人通りの絶えた道を、今もなお静かに照らし続ける、一つの灯り。その温かな光は、道行く人の心をそっと包み込むかのようです。」 The right one reads beautifully and says nothing Peter said.

exitImage.description: On the board Peter's caption stands mended — one verb form changed, the closing question 「だれのためだろう」 still there. Sophie's polished rewrite is folded to one side, kept but no longer the version on show. Nothing of his has been overwritten.

propCues.description: The change is split into two columns: an ERROR column holding only 「がつけている → がついている」, and a VOICE column holding the words and the question that must stay untouched — 「だれのためだろう」. Whichever the last attempt over-changed comes back for another try; what was kept correctly stays put.

scenes.goal: Turn one over-fix into a class practice: point out an error as advice, and change a voice only with its author's consent.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Can help stop before it becomes speaking for someone — by asking first?
scenes.learnerNeed: A stance choice about how a correction is offered so that fixing the error stays separate from, and never presumes, the right to rewrite the voice.

intents: Propose the practice: point out an error as advice with 〜ほうがいいと思います and leave the change to the writer, because touching a voice is a separate request from correcting a mistake — ask before touching it.
Deliver the correction as an offer Peter can decline, and name that finding an error never came with the right to rewrite — leaving the choice is what keeps the correction kind.
Take the advice and make the single change in his own hand, keep his closing question, and note that a correction offered this way is one he actually wants to make.

openingImage.description: Peter's mended caption is pinned up. Beside it lies a blank slip headed 提案 ("suggestion"), and Sophie's folded polished version rests further off — available if Peter ever wants it, imposed on nothing. The question on the table is how corrections should be offered from now on.

exitImage.description: Peter's caption now carries the single fix in his own hand, his closing question still standing. Sophie's polished version stays folded to one side, offered but not imposed. On the suggestion slip a small class rule is written: 間違いは伝える。声は、訊いてから。 ("Point out the error; the voice, only after asking.") Nothing has been overwritten.

scenes.goal: Meet Sam mid-draft as the venue's deadline pushes him toward re-asking the silent contributors, and reach the point where adding options can no longer make the request kinder.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: When a public version is wanted before everyone has agreed, will Sam chase the missing yeses or build one request that makes 'no' easy to give?
scenes.learnerNeed: A composed request that names the event and its scope and, in the same sentence, leaves a real and easy way to decline.

intents: Relay the venue's deadline and, under the pressure of it, propose re-asking the two who have gone quiet and adding one easier option so the yes comes faster.
Drop the re-ask and the extra option, and commit to asking once — with what and how far stated as scope, and an easy decline folded into the same sentence.
Read the composed request aloud — one sentence that names the event and the scope and, in the same breath, makes 'not yet' an easy answer — and notice that this makes declining easy on purpose.
Point out that re-asking and stacking options makes refusal harder, not easier, and that a request must carry its scope and an easy 'no' inside the same sentence.

openingImage.description: On the cafe table, beside the drinks Sam has already set out, sits the venue's message: the public evening wants a shareable version of the exhibition captions by the weekend. Sam's draft invitation to the contributors is open on his phone, and it has grown three follow-ups long — a second way to ask, a spare option, a gentle nudge for the two who have not replied.

exitImage.description: Sam sends the one message and closes the draft. The three follow-ups are gone from it; only the single scoped request stands in the thread, an easy 'not yet' sitting inside it. The drinks stay on the table, untouched, waiting.

propCues.description: The draft request is laid out with its two parts underlined: the scope line and the decline line. Only the part that was missing returns for another try — a request without a stated range, or one with no easy way to say no — while the part that already worked stays in place.

scenes.goal: Let a contributor's 'not yet' arrive and change the plan, so the public version is redesigned to carry only consented material instead of arguing the missing yes into place.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: When one contributor says 'not yet,' will the class chase a better yes or rebuild the page around the answer it was given?
scenes.learnerNeed: A stance choice about how a public page should hold a part that cannot be shown yet, without treating a heard 'no' as a problem to solve.

intents: Feel the pull to soften the no with one more small question, stop himself, accept 'not yet' as a complete answer, and turn to what the plan must become instead.
Extend from this one caption to the whole public atlas — it carries only consented material and points to the terms for the rest, which is what keeps it honest rather than one owned story.
Close the evening by leaving the door open for the person who said 'not yet' — their space is kept, offered again only if they choose, with no pursuit.
Reframe the scoped page not as a lesser version but as the more honest, more precise one, and name asking-once-with-an-exit as the way the class works now.

openingImage.description: A reply lands on the table between them. One of the two has answered — 「まだ、名前は出さないでほしい」, not yet, please don't use my name. The part of the caption that belongs to that person now cannot go on the public page. The venue's deadline is still Saturday.

exitImage.description: The public page is set with only the consented captions, one space left marked 'under discussion' with its condition written beside it. The venue has its version by Saturday; the withheld part is not on it. Sam's single reply to the 'not yet' sits sent and quiet, no pursuit behind it. Only now do the two of them pick up the drinks that have been waiting on the table.

title.ja: その椅子は空けておく

scenes.goal: Reach the moment Jenny declines the visible guide role and the group's first instinct is to solve the empty seat for her.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: When someone declines a visible role, will the class shrink the role to pull them back, or hear the no and change the plan?
scenes.learnerNeed: A changed-context task where redesigning the evening around a stated limit matters more than finding a better way to persuade.

intents: Offer Jenny the visible front-of-house guide role while naming the activity plainly and making a decline genuinely easy in the same breath.
Reflexively treat the empty seat as a gap to close by shrinking the front role so Jenny can still be coaxed into it — the well-meaning instinct the scene has to correct.
Decline the visible role softly and name the back-of-house role she does want, without over-explaining or offering a justifying reason.
Accept the redesign, take the back-of-house role as a full contribution rather than a lesser one, and turn her knitting-repair on the plan's shape — not on her own visibility.

openingImage.description: The exhibition-evening plan is chalked on the board as a row of role cards. One card reads 「案内役 — 前に立って地図を説明する」 with a blank name line. Jenny is in her usual seat, a half-finished scarf on her lap, one needle resting mid-row.

exitImage.description: A new card now sits on the back-of-house side: 「進行・道具の段取り — ジェニー」. The guide-role card keeps its blank name line, uncrossed. Jenny's needle has moved on a row; the scarf is a little longer.

propCues.description: Two drafted responses sit side by side on the board: one that trims the front role to coax Jenny back, one that leaves the front seat open and builds a full role from the back. Only the persuade-shaped response returns for another pass; the redesign-shaped one stays where it is.

scenes.goal: Decide how to hold the open guide seat so support reads as redesign, not a seat kept warm for Jenny's return.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Can an open chair be a finished plan rather than an unfilled gap waiting for the person who declined it?
scenes.learnerNeed: A stance choice about whether an open role is an invitation left genuinely open or a front dissolved so no single narrator is needed.

intents: Frame the open guide seat as something to keep open on purpose rather than have Jenny fill, while admitting a bare blank feels unfinished and asking how to hold it open well.
Name that the empty chair is neither reserved for Jenny's return nor a hole to plug out of anxiety, and that rebuilding the plan around it is what support actually is.
Mark the guide seat as deliberately open and point the day's flow into Jenny's back-of-house running order, closing without filling the chair.
Widen from the seat to the atlas: showing the map was never one person's job at the front, so an open chair does not leave it unspoken — the back-of-house work is a real part of the telling.

openingImage.description: The board is redrawn clean. The back-of-house role reads 「ジェニー」. The guide-role card still stands, its name line blank — not scribbled out, not reassigned, simply open.

exitImage.description: The guide-role card keeps its blank name line with a small note beside it — 「空けたまま」. The back-of-house card reads 「ジェニー」, its role written out in full. Nothing on the board is crossed out, and the scarf on Jenny's lap has grown one even row longer.

scenes.goal: Set two complete, conflicting event schedules beside each other and reach the point where 'whose list is better' can no longer decide the date.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: When two plans are both defensible, will the class rank one document over the other, or separate what was confirmed from what was only heard?
scenes.learnerNeed: A way to sort each claim in two schedules into confirmed evidence, heard hearsay, and sequence, and to state aloud the assumption the whole disagreement rests on.

intents: State his version flatly as Thursday, but immediately mark the seam himself: he confirmed it once, then heard it may have changed, so 'Thursday' is not yet a certainty.

Take the disagreement off the 'which list is better' axis and onto its real seam: his Thursday is confirmed evidence, her Friday rests on a heard change, and the two are lumped together under one word. Propose separating confirmed from heard before deciding, with no winner.
Present her spreadsheet as the settled, gapless plan for Friday and treat the completeness of the list as reason enough to proceed, without auditing where the Friday itself came from.

Accept, without collapse, that her list was gapless in its contents but rested on a Friday premise she never audited — she treated a heard change as fact and built on it. Name the assumption plainly; the list is still good, its foundation was assumed.

openingImage.description: On the classroom table, two versions of the exhibition-event plan lie side by side. One is Alex's hand-ruled timetable, headed 木曜 (Thursday). One is Angel's printed spreadsheet, every row filled, headed 金曜 (Friday). Times, roles, and order run down both. Neither is crossed out.

exitImage.description: Both schedules stay on the table, still neither crossed out. A new narrow column has been added down each — headed もと (basis) — and every row now carries a tag: 確認 (confirmed) or 聞いた (heard). The two dates, Thursday and Friday, sit at the top of columns that no longer pretend to be the same kind of thing.

propCues.description: The three columns — confirmed, heard, and sequence — stand where they were filled. Only the one claim that was tagged to the wrong column slides back out for another read; the correctly sorted rows stay put, and the stated assumption remains written at the top.

scenes.goal: Draft one clarified plan that states its assumption, keeps the date provisional, and assigns who confirms the heard change — without declaring either schedule the winner.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Can a plan hold two defensible dates by naming its condition, instead of overwriting one into a single 'correct' schedule?
scenes.learnerNeed: A stance on how a clarified plan should hold the two dates — as a written condition, or as a provisional pair with one assigned confirmation step.

intents: Frame the clarified plan so the assumption is written openly and the date-decision is handed to whoever can confirm the change with the source, rather than her completed list silently deciding it. End on a real consent check.

Widen from this one schedule to the atlas: like the plan, it need not be overwritten into a single correct version — it can carry its conditions and its not-yet-confirmed parts openly. Name her own turn: leaving the provisional provisional is as proper as filling everything in.

Reframe the plan as no verdict on who was right — his calm Thursday was not more true, only differently sourced. Name the class practice plainly: write the assumption, decline to declare a winner. His growth narrows him to fewer, flatter words, not eloquence.

Close the evening flat and few-worded: leave the date open and provisional, ask once to regather after the confirmation, and let the plan stand without a winner. The calmest possible delivery carries the whole resolution.

openingImage.description: A third, blank sheet lies between the two tagged schedules. It is ruled into the same rows but carries an extra column headed 前提 (assumption). The two original plans stay beside it, unchanged; this one is meant to hold what they were both quietly resting on.

exitImage.description: The two original schedules stay on the table, neither crossed out. Between them the clarified sheet holds the assumption in its own column and the date line left open, marked 仮 (provisional), with one name beside a single step: confirm the heard change. Nothing declares a winner; the plan simply names what it is still waiting on.

scenes.goal: Examine how a 'clearer' subtitle erased a hedge the interviewee actually made, and separate the quote from the claim.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: When a subtitle reads better than the source, whose words are we hearing?
scenes.learnerNeed: A way to keep what a speaker actually said, hedge and all, apart from what a translation claims on their behalf.

intents: Bring an interview clip instead of a drama and point out that the official subtitle reads more decisively than the voice underneath it actually commits to.
Name that the subtitle asserted a certainty the speaker never made, using her signature challenge to the over-definitive cut.
Invite the learner to re-subtitle the blank track to carry the speaker's hedge, and state plainly that it is someone else's words with an easy decline.
Draw the line between what the speaker literally said (a quotable hedge) and what the subtitle now claims for her, and require that quoting stop where the evidence stops.

openingImage.description: The library's back corner is dark except for a paused interview frame: a woman mid-answer, looking slightly off-camera. Two subtitle tracks are stacked under it — one labelled OFFICIAL, reading cleanly; one blank, waiting. Ruparna stands by the screen with the transcript in her hand, not the remote.

exitImage.description: Two captions now stand side by side under the paused frame: OFFICIAL, reading 「はい、その通りです」, and the class's rewrite, which keeps the 「たぶん」 and the 「はっきりとは覚えていない」. Neither is pretending to be the other. The clean version reads better. The honest version reads truer.

propCues.description: Ruparna plays the line. In the audio the woman says, haltingly, 「たぶん、そうだったと思うんですけど…正直、はっきりとは覚えていなくて」. Under it the OFFICIAL track reads, in confident type: 「はい、その通りです」. The hesitation in the voice and the certainty in the caption sit on screen at the same time.

Only the one clause where the new caption crept back toward certainty is highlighted — a 「〜んです」 that reads a shade firmer than the voice earned. The rest of the rewrite stays on screen; just that clause waits, with the audio queued to replay once more so the hedge can be matched exactly.

scenes.goal: Decide what the honest caption may claim, and refuse to publish the smoother version even though it would read better for the exhibition.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Is the seventy-percent door still a door when the missing part is not ours to open?
scenes.learnerNeed: A stance that preserves the speaker's uncertainty rather than filling it, and a plan that survives one person's refusal.

intents: Tally what the interview actually established — only that the speaker said she does not remember — and reverse the seventy-percent rule: the unknown thirty is hers, not a gap for the subtitle to fill.

Decline to sign off on publishing the smoother official version for the exhibition, even though it reads better, and treat that certainty as the speaker's to give, not the class's to supply — one clear refusal, no room read as coldness.

Accept Sophie's refusal without arguing it back, redesign the exhibition plan around the honest caption, and reframe her seventy-percent door as a limit — preserving the hedge is now a duty, not a preference.

openingImage.description: The clip holds on the woman's off-camera glance. Sophie caps the marker and steps back so both captions are readable at once. Under the honest rewrite she has written a single short line: 確実に言えること — and the space after it is deliberately small.

exitImage.description: The OFFICIAL caption is dragged into a folder marked 'not used.' Under the paused frame, only the honest rewrite remains — the 「たぶん」 and the 「はっきりとは覚えていない」 left standing in plain type. The clean sentence that would have read better is gone, and the speaker's uncertainty is the thing the class chose to carry.

title.en: The Right Screen, the Wrong Draft
title.ja: 画面は正しく、原稿は古い

scenes.goal: Catch that the rehearsal screen is showing an obsolete internal draft with a withdrawn passage, and repair the state before urgency turns access into exposure.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: With the wrong version already on screen and the rehearsal clock running, does the class swap the file fast, or stop to confirm which draft is live and whether this passage may be shown at all?
scenes.learnerNeed: A state-check where naming which version is prepared-and-live and attributing the claim to the document matters more than a thirty-second fix.

intents: Front-load that the screen is supposed to be the prepared, standing version, then discover the assumption is wrong — this is the superseded internal draft, and it still carries the withdrawn passage.

Stop the fast overwrite; separate being able to reach the file from being allowed to show it; propose confirming which draft is live and containing the withdrawn passage before anything is changed or displayed, attributing the claim to the document rather than to a person.

Give the immediate, plain procedural apology and name the repair — she loaded the old internal draft by mistake, she has now put the live version back, and the withdrawn passage was not shown — attributing the error to the version rather than to any person.
Reach for the mechanism — offer to overwrite the file back to the live version in seconds under the rehearsal clock — then qualify the real risk only a beat late.

openingImage.description: On the rehearsal screen the exhibition caption block loads on cue. One line inside it is a passage the class formally withdrew during review — it was supposed to be gone. No one has read it aloud, and the rehearsal timer is running in the corner.

exitImage.description: The live version stands on the rehearsal screen; the withdrawn passage is covered and was never read aloud. Without a word, Tom sets a small version stamp on the corner of the live file and moves the old draft into a separate, labelled place, so the two can no longer be confused for each other.

propCues.description: A group-chat notification slides in from Mira, following along from the chat: can't we just swap the file back and keep the rehearsal going, we're on the clock. It is the fast-fix instinct arriving as pressure — not as permission — while the timer keeps counting.

Two versions sit side by side, neither one displayed: the prepared, standing live version and the superseded internal draft. Only the step that went wrong returns — matching the evidential marker to the correct version, or covering the withdrawn passage — while the parts already handled stay as they are.

scenes.goal: Turn the contained incident into the class's standing rule — internal access is not permission — and record which version is live alongside what may be shown, keeping the withdrawn passage's place without its content.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: With the draft contained, does the class file this as a version bug it patched, or write down that access was never permission and keep the withdrawn passage's place without its content?
scenes.learnerNeed: A stance choice about whether the record should hold the incident as version discipline or as a consent boundary, and the realization that it must hold both.

intents: Frame the note as recording two separate things — which version is prepared-and-live, and what the class may actually show — and name that being able to reach a file was never the same as permission to display it.

Unify the two framings — version discipline and consent are two separate locks, and even a prepared, reachable version is not permission; attribute claims to the document, hedge what cannot be confirmed, and name this as how the class will handle a wrong-draft load from now on.

Instead of arguing for the fast swap, redesign the tool — build a confirm-which-version-is-live check before rehearsal starts and write it down so someone else can run it without him — so the workaround is never the first move again.

openingImage.description: A note page lies open beside the laptop, ruled into two columns: one headed for which version is live, one headed for what may be shown. In the second column, the withdrawn passage has a marked slot, left deliberately blank.

exitImage.description: The live version stands stamped on the screen; the old draft sits quarantined in its own labelled place. The note is filled in two columns — which version is live, and what may be shown — with the withdrawn passage's slot marked and left blank. Along the bottom, one line: access is not permission. Nothing withdrawn was ever displayed, and the chat's fast-swap urging was never acted on.

title.ja: 言えること、言えないこと

scenes.goal: Reach the moment the class stops treating Jodi's memory as automatic public authority and separates memory, evidence, and permission before writing the caption.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: When someone was truly there, does being the source of a memory settle what may be published about it?
scenes.learnerNeed: A calibration task where tagging how each claim is known, and writing only the permitted version, matters more than repeating the confident one.

intents: Stop the class from publishing her memory as flat fact; name that she remembers it clearly, but remembering, being able to show, and being permitted to publish are three separate things.
Propose the method: mark each claim by how it is known (saw, heard, inferred), write the two times she always keeps, add a confidence tier, and publish only what has both evidence and permission.
Accept the calibrated, permission-scoped public sentence; mark confidence honestly; keep the first-person memory as memory to hand to one chosen person, not as published fact.

Deliver the quiet ruling turned against her own authority: even the person who decides what is real Japanese finds that being the source of a phrase or a memory is not permission to publish it. Soft, no display.

openingImage.description: On the cafe table sits the draft public caption for the exhibition, next to Jodi's old Tokyo photograph: a narrow street, a small shop long gone. Beside them Rose has laid down the page she physically found, the unattributed old caption. Someone has written the draft in confident plain style, 「この角には昔パン屋があった」, as flat established fact, with a margin note: since Jodi was there, just write it.

exitImage.description: The public draft now reads with its source marked and its confidence shown; the first-person 'I saw it' line is gone from the wall copy. Jodi's Tokyo photograph is turned face-down beside her, kept, not displayed. Rose's found page stays on the table as material the class can show — but nothing on it is claimed as anyone's story.

propCues.description: The draft is laid out with three evidence tags beside it — saw / heard / inferred — and a confidence mark. Only the claims still written as flat fact return for another pass; the ones already source-marked and permission-scoped stay as they are.

scenes.goal: Stress-test the calibrated rule against a real visitor's question and let the class settle on publishing only what is verified and permitted, holding memory plural and owned by no single person.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Does a careful rule about what may be said survive the moment a stranger asks whether it was real?
scenes.learnerNeed: A stance choice about whether the public version marks the memory with evidence and permission, or withholds it and publishes only what the material page supports.

intents: Stress-test the rule the way she stress-tests a study app: does it work in ordinary use, or just look careful? Name the concrete visitor's question it has to survive.
Reframe hedging as the grammar of not overclaiming rather than weakness; confirm the permission-scoped version is what they publish and that it survives being asked on the day.
Close the exchange cleanly, her signature: name what goes on the wall and what stays with each owner, warmly and without lingering.
Widen from the caption to the whole atlas: it was layered by many hands, so keeping each person able to say how far a memory is theirs is more accurate than naming one owner.

openingImage.description: The calibrated draft sits between them; on a propped-up phone the group chat is open, and Mira has typed in from Miami, half English and half Japanese, asking whether the careful rule they just made actually holds up when a real visitor pushes on it.

exitImage.description: The public draft is finalized: each line carries how it is known and how sure, and only what was verified and permitted is on it. Jodi's photograph stays face-down beside her, hers to share or not. On the phone, Mira's group-chat reply reads simply that it will hold. Rose's found page remains as shared material; nothing on it is signed as anyone's story.

scenes.goal: Meet the empty host slot the night before the run-through and reach a redistribution of the public role that coerces no one.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: When the person at the front is gone, does the class push someone forward, or build a role a quiet person can choose?
scenes.learnerNeed: A role negotiation where offering a job, naming its exit, and honouring a 'not yet' matters more than filling the microphone.

intents: Instead of shouldering the empty host slot herself, thank the volunteers and split the job into named roles, each offered with an easy decline.
Turn Mika's idea into an actual offer, modelling the negotiation shape the learner will run: state the job, put an easy no and a way out in the same breath, and make either answer fine.

After a beat of silence, reframe the empty microphone: the front is not the only real role, and his old pause-and-count can become an offstage cue so a person who does not want the mic can still hold a public-facing job.
Confirm the redistributed roles, take the offstage cue himself as a chosen role, and name his familiar step-back as a deliberate handoff now, not a retreat.

openingImage.description: The classroom is set up for the exhibition run-through: a microphone stands alone at the front, and a run sheet on the board lists every job but leaves the host line blank — the person who was to host cannot come. Rie's tea sits cold on the side desk. Three classmates have half-raised their hands to cover, glancing at the quietest people in the room.

exitImage.description: The run sheet now carries a name beside every job, with a new offstage cue role written in among them. The microphone still stands unclaimed at the front — but it reads as an open place now, not a hole someone must be pushed into filling.

propCues.description: Only the one job whose offer landed wrong comes back for another pass — re-phrased so the exit is unmistakable this time. The roles already agreed, each with its stated way out, stay assigned on the run sheet; no one who said 'not yet' is asked again.

scenes.goal: Run the rehearsal, let the backstage cue repair a live miss without blame, and decide how the quiet role is recorded.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Is an offstage cue a small favour, or a full role worth writing down beside the microphone?
scenes.learnerNeed: A stance on whether a quiet, offstage contribution is named as full participation or kept deliberately un-spotlighted at the person's own preference.

intents: Repair the missed entrance from offstage with the count, keep the run going, and name the miss as a timing slip that belongs to no one — spontaneous repair without blame.
Name the season's turn: a quiet role is not the hole left by someone missing but a role chosen and held; and his own step-back is now a handoff he stays to watch land.
Point out that the offstage cue held the whole run together, and ask to record it on the sheet at the same weight as the microphone role.
Accept that the room runs without her holding every thread, and hand the closing to someone else — accepting a specific handoff rather than absorbing the last job herself.

openingImage.description: The rehearsal runs. Mika stands in the wing with the run sheet and a quiet hand ready to count. The mic is live at the front, but no one is being held to it. Partway through, an entrance is missed — a half-second of dead air — and the room tenses.

exitImage.description: The run sheet holds the offstage cue role — named in full beside the host, or kept in the internal notes at the person's own request, whichever the class chose. The microphone stays on its stand, unclaimed and unforced, because the role that held the evening together was never the mic. Every 'yes' on the sheet was chosen; every 'no' left a real exit.

scenes.goal: Examine the ownerless page as physical evidence and reach the point where reading the characters cannot answer who wrote it.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: When the class wants a name to close the mystery, will decoding produce an author, or will the material only support a qualified account of stewardship?
scenes.learnerNeed: A way to compare paper, ink, and version traces across a record and state a conclusion qualified to exactly what the evidence supports.

intents: Read the characters with obvious ease but flip his own joke — the reading is easy, the history is not — and order the writing hands by stroke habit without naming a single one.
Start from the physical object — paper weight, sun-fade, ink colour by layer — and only then widen to the long view, turning the question from who is the author to how the page was handed down.
Name exactly how far the material reaches — composition, dating, and order — and hold her binding limit: proof of the material is not permission to name a person or narrate their story.

openingImage.description: The old unattributed caption page from the atlas backing is laid flat under the library lamp. Beside it sit two things Felix brought: the small paper cat marker, and his own quiet log of where that marker has rested across successive terms — column after column of dates and positions, kept but never explained. Under a loupe the caption is not one clean hand: the ink darkens and lightens down the sheet, and the paper itself is thicker at the bottom than at the top.

exitImage.description: The page's layers now lie in reconstructed order, oldest and sun-faded at the base, whitest on top. The paper cat rests on the seam between two of them. The margin beside the caption is still empty of any name.

propCues.description: The layers the learner already ordered stay lined up in sequence. Only the one trace whose claim outran its evidence returns — an over-confident line quietly re-set beside the paper and ink it was supposed to rest on, waiting to be stated again at the strength the record actually supports.

scenes.goal: Decide what the margin will record when the class wants a name but the evidence supports only a qualified account of stewardship.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Can a blank name column and a qualified note be more honest than a single name that closes the mystery too soon?
scenes.learnerNeed: A stance on recording a source comparison as a conclusion qualified to the evidence, without naming a person the record cannot support.

intents: Refuse to write a single name, state why the evidence and the ethics both stop her, and redesign the plan — leave the name field blank and record only what the evidence supports.
Widen from the single page to the whole atlas: no owner, but tended by many across years, so the class's job is to receive and pass on rather than to sign a name.

Return his suspended joke transformed — the reading was easy, the history is not — and read the paper cat's placement as version evidence, stating the conclusion by source comparison at qualified confidence.

openingImage.description: A fresh index card sits beside the page, ruled into two fields: one headed 'name,' one headed 'what the record supports.' A pencil rests across it. The paper cat still marks the seam between the layers, quietly turning from a mascot into the point where one class's writing hands off to the next.

exitImage.description: The index card's 'name' field stays blank on purpose. In the field beside it sits the qualified conclusion — several hands, over years, in order, no author named. The paper cat rests on the seam between two layers as a version-index rather than a mascot, marking where one class handed the page to the next. Nothing is claimed beyond what the record supports.

scenes.goal: Sit the class down to author the permission page and reach the point where the passages nobody can be asked for cannot honestly be marked permitted.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: When a passage has no contributor to ask, will the class invent an owner to fill the page or withhold it on purpose?
scenes.learnerNeed: A formal-writing task where sorting each passage by whether consent actually stands matters more than filling every cell of the page.

intents: Name exactly what the page must record — who may share which passage, for which event, and for how long — and build in that any contributor can decline any part in a single word.

Propose the page's rule — record who/event/expiry only where consent stands; where there is no one to ask or the answer is a soft not-yet, the passage stays withheld rather than published, and the plan changes to fit that.
Name that withholding what cannot be consented is a chosen, honest act rather than a failure to finish, and that with it the public evening can go ahead responsibly.
Turn the terms into a legible document of state, condition, and expiry, then name the wall — the passages with no identifiable contributor have no one to ask, so they cannot be marked permitted.

openingImage.description: On the long classroom table the margin-study records are laid out: paper folds, ink shades, and the marker's positions across several successive classes, showing a page layered by many hands with no single owner. Beside them lies a blank sheet headed 「公開の許可」 with three empty columns — who may share, for which event, and until when. A short stack of passages sits apart under a paper slip reading 「保留」, the lines no contributor could be named for. A group-chat note left open on a phone reminds the room, in Nanako's words, that any request they send must carry an easy way to say no.

exitImage.description: The permission page now carries a filled column of consented passages — each with a name, an event, and a date — and a sealed withheld section holding the rest, marked only 「保留」 with no invented author. A short line at the foot points to the contributors' terms. The public version is, for the first time, safe to show.

propCues.description: The passages are set out in two groups: a permitted column carrying who / which event / until when, and the withheld slip holding the rest, unlabelled by any invented owner. Only the passage that was sorted into the wrong group returns for another pass; the correctly sorted ones stay where they are.

scenes.goal: Let the class settle how long each permission holds and how sure it is, so the page is both usable and honest, and close the season without inventing a permanent yes.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Can a page that names its own expiry and confidence carry more trust than one that claims a flat forever?
scenes.learnerNeed: A stance choice about whether a permission should be recorded as permanent or as a term that names its confidence and expiry.

intents: Frame each term as carrying a confidence and an expiry, so the page is honest — a permission that names its limits is stronger than one stated flat.
Reframe precision as marking a term's limits — expiry and confidence — rather than claiming a flat permanent yes, and name it as the page's practice going forward.

Close by naming what the page makes possible — a public evening on consented material only — and leave the door open for contributors to extend their terms later, asking once and not pressing anyone now.

openingImage.description: The permission page lies open beside the class's number notebook, with its two columns of claims kept alongside their context. Sophie sets three coloured marks down the page's margin: one for a permission that is certain, one for a term that should be re-confirmed later, and one for the withheld passages that stay closed.

exitImage.description: The permission page is complete: consented passages each carry a name, an event, an expiry, and a coloured confidence mark; the withheld section stays sealed under 「保留」 with no invented owner; a foot-line points to the contributors' terms. Nothing has been assigned to a person who did not agree, and the public evening is now possible.

scenes.goal: Read the former learner's selective reply and reach the point where the class must decide whether to chase the gaps or accept a bounded, partly-declined answer.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: When a reply answers some questions, quietly skips one, and openly refuses another, will the class pry at the gaps or read the omission as an answer in itself?
scenes.learnerNeed: A changed-context transfer where sorting a formal reply into answered, left-unsaid, and declined, then reading what the omission and refusal mean, matters more than extracting every withheld fact.

intents: Name the shape of the reply before its content: some answered, one left unmentioned, one openly declined. Then say he wants to read where the line was drawn, the way he reads a work email.
Before writing anything back, propose sorting the reply into answered, left-unsaid, and declined — and read the omission as deliberate, not an oversight.

Read the sorted reply: the former learner told the class exactly what they'll confirm and where they'll stop, so the omission and the decline read as authored, not accidental. Close on a quiet 'splendid.'
Flat and itemized: a formal decline is a complete answer, not a dodge; you record it and don't chase it, the way he writes one at work.
Flat — the way the reply was returned is already the answer; there's no need to send it back asking more.

openingImage.description: A rain-spotted envelope has arrived with the class's five questions folded inside the reply. Three answers are numbered in the margin. Number four is absent. Beside number five, one sentence stands alone: 「その理由については、お答えしかねます」. Peter has taken the window seat nobody noticed was occupied and set three paper clips beside the page.

exitImage.description: The reply's parts lie in three columns now: answered, left unsaid, declined. Only the line that went into the wrong column comes back. The rest stay where they are.

scenes.goal: Compose a follow-up that accepts the bounded reply — thank what was given, press nothing withheld, and decide how to treat the one declined question.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Can a reply that presses nothing still be a complete, adult answer?
scenes.learnerNeed: A stance choice about whether the follow-up sets the declined question down for good or leaves one easy door open without pressure.

intents: Frame the follow-up: thank them for what they gave, touch nothing they withheld, keep it in keigo — a reply that accepts the bounded answer without reopening it.
Seal the follow-up and file the declined question in the record as declined, not as a blank or unfinished business. Close the evening quietly.
Flat and even, no lift in the voice: a bounded no, taken as a no, costs nothing, and the letter stands complete either way. A keigo refusal, in his mouth, still lands warm.

openingImage.description: A blank sheet beside the sorted reply. The declined question sits by itself in the short column. Nobody has started the follow-up.

exitImage.description: The follow-up goes out in an envelope noticeably thinner than the one that arrived. Peter clips the three confirmed answers to the letter; number four remains marked 'not stated,' and number five 'declined, not to be reopened.' On top he places one card for tomorrow's evidence map: earlier learner added one route; space left intentionally. The other contributor fields stay untouched.

scenes.goal: Lay out three sources of unequal reliability and reach the point where merging them into one account would mean inventing what the record cannot support.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Faced with sources that disagree, will the class write one clean story, or a map that keeps each claim at its true confidence?
scenes.learnerNeed: A synthesis task where sorting each claim to its source and marking how sure it is matters more than producing a single finished account.

intents: Spread the three sources as a finishable job and lean toward pulling them into one clean account tonight, her finish-first reflex reaching for a single story.

Take the turn away from one account and toward a map where every claim carries its source and its confidence, giving her colour-coding the new job and naming the diagnostic level 'this only goes as far as apparently.'
Point to two dark-green cards with different sources and ask Sophie to label source separately from certainty.
Check that each colour matches its source status, then catch his old impulse to add a pale tab merely to make the grid look complete.

openingImage.description: The library closing bell is forty minutes away. Across the long table, Sophie's coloured tabs already make a confident-looking grid: the former learner's letter, paper and ink samples from the old page, and the class's notes. Two claims in the front row carry the same dark green, though one comes from direct testimony and the other from a mark on paper. Henry has stopped with one finger between them.

exitImage.description: A large sheet now covers the table, ruled into cells. Each filled cell carries a coloured tab and a short source line under it. One cell near the middle is left uncoloured, a single phrase written across it and nothing else.

propCues.description: Only the one cell whose confidence tag outran its source is lifted back out. Its coloured tab is set to the side while the source line under it is read again, slower. The cells already placed stay exactly where they are.

scenes.goal: Finish the legend before closing time and decide how it distinguishes a claim unsupported by any source from a question the former learner expressly declined.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Will the map keep 'no source found' and 'the source declined' visibly distinct when the venue asks for one clean answer?
scenes.learnerNeed: A stance on holding a claim the record cannot support and a person chose not to answer, keeping both facts visible.

intents: Name the labelled blank as the strongest cell on the map, mark her own change from wanting every cell filled, and tie the whole map back to the number notebook as its grown-up form.
Weigh the two sources against each other, conclude only to the level the record supports, and set the map's line as the way the class will one day close the atlas.

Commit to building the map's data so blanks stay blank on screen and versions are dated, changed behavior after the wrong-draft incident: the tool itself now shows where it is uncertain rather than smoothing it over.

openingImage.description: The map is nearly full. In the middle, one uncoloured cell carries a source line instead of a claim: absent from every record checked. Sophie's old two-column notebook is wedged under the ruler, keeping the new grid from curling.

exitImage.description: The closing bell sounds. Under the reading lamp, every claim now carries two separate marks: a source line and a confidence shade. Henry's screen matches the paper grid exactly. As Sophie caps her darkest pen, the library printer wakes and produces the venue's final-panel request: one founder, one clean ending. She lays it face-down on the finished legend for tomorrow.

scenes.goal: Reach the moment Robert stops trying to satisfy the venue by adding, and commits to a refusal that keeps the relationship.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Offered the chance to fill one more gap, will Robert add the ending the venue wants or decline the one the evidence can't hold?
scenes.learnerNeed: A composed keigo refusal that concedes the venue's intent, holds the boundary, and offers one clear alternative instead of more options.

intents: Read the venue's polite ask aloud, welcome it warmly, then reach straight for his old reflex — satisfy it by adding a closing line, a founder's name, a photo.

Catch his own reflex, set the pen down, and switch from adding to declining — name the shape of the reply (concede, refuse, offer one alternative, leave room) and ask the learner to put it into words.
Read the composed refusal back, commit to it as the ending the class can stand behind, keep the warmth toward the venue, and stop — add nothing more.
Stop the additions by pointing at the one cell the class left blank on purpose — a single founder would be a fact they don't have — and ask, once, whether the honest move is to decline.
Back the refusal from the other side of the table — it is easy for the venue to receive because it does not end at 'no' but sets down one clear next move with room to answer.

openingImage.description: The cafe's long table is covered by the public-evening proof. The venue's courteous request for one founder and a more moving close is circled in red. Before anyone has taken off a coat, Robert has opened three attachment windows: a founder label, a photograph, and an extra closing caption.

exitImage.description: Robert closes all three attachment windows. The reply now holds one concession, one no, and one alternative. Sam slides the evidence legend under the laptop where its source lines remain visible; the venue has one specific proposal to answer.

propCues.description: The three moves are laid out as cards along the table edge: a concession, a refusal, and one alternative with an open line beneath it. Only the move the learner left out returns for another pass; the cards already placed stay where they are.

scenes.goal: Let the reply leave the venue real room to answer, so a refusal opens a conversation instead of closing one.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Can a 'no' be sent once, without chasing, and still keep the relationship warm?
scenes.learnerNeed: A stance on how much room a polite refusal should leave for the other side to decide.

intents: Frame the sending: one message, no chasing, wait for the venue's answer — and make sure the warmth, that the class still wants to do this with them, survives a letter that says no.
Land the payoff plainly and warmly, without a joke — the strength came from what Robert didn't add — then move to send it the once and wait.
Name what he learned in the act, not as a lesson but as a surprise — the strongest reply is the one he didn't fill, and a courteous no is a different thing from a cold one.

openingImage.description: The reply is ready on Robert's laptop, its subject line unchanged. On the proof beside it, the founder box has become one question. Robert's cursor hovers over Send while Sam turns the three unused printouts face-down.

exitImage.description: The reply goes out once, with no attachments. Robert caps his pen; Sam turns his phone face-down. On the proof, the final panel ends on a question rather than a founder. The venue's answer is now the only item still pending.

scenes.goal: Reach the three non-matching accounts of how the first page began and the moment picking one becomes impossible, so the class must decide how to hold three descriptions of one origin.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: When three people describe the same beginning three different ways, will the class rank one as real or keep all three as vantage points?
scenes.learnerNeed: A stance on three accounts that clash in wording but not in truth, where naming why each holds matters more than choosing the correct one.

intents: Notice that three notes about one beginning don't agree, and rather than rush to resolve them, say plainly that this kind of mismatch has never troubled her.
Propose not ranking the three but reading them as three vantage points on one beginning (each person's start is the point they entered), so all three can be true at once.
Name her own long habit (writing two times over one place and deleting neither) as the same move now scaled to three, marking the changed behavior after her limit.
Give one calibrated, non-defensive account of the beginning she remembers, vouching only for what she saw and refusing to claim it was the very first mark.

openingImage.description: Three transparent sheets disagree before anyone speaks. One shows Rie's blank template, one the route already present when the former learner received it, and one the class's page accumulating marks. A desk fan lifts their corners; Jodi pins each with a different coloured clip beside the atlas's first page.

exitImage.description: Jodi labels the second clip 'when the former learner received it' and the third 'when this class began counting.' The three transparent sheets still show different page states, but they no longer pretend to describe the same instant. The interval between Rie's handoff and the letter remains unwitnessed.

scenes.goal: Turn three kept accounts into one synthesis that says why all three can be true without flattening any speaker, and leave the beginning plural with no omniscient correction.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Can one sentence hold three clashing accounts as compatible truths without shrinking any of them into a footnote?
scenes.learnerNeed: A recognition check where the learner identifies the synthesis that attributes all three accounts and leaves the unwitnessed interval open.

intents: Ask, before the synthesis, that her account stay one among several and not be enlarged by her teacher role, modelling that memory is not authority.
Close without defending or ruling: keep only what she can vouch for, leave the unseen span open rather than force it shut, and set who fills it later as a question not yet to be decided.
Name the task: bind the three into one telling with each voice kept, using embedded-quotation markers, holding the clash rather than erasing it.
Confirm the synthesis holds with all three voices intact, and say that keeping three true versions is more accurate than choosing one real beginning, with nobody's beginning crossed out.

openingImage.description: The three transparent sheets are clipped to one backing page, each headed by its speaker and entry point. The unwitnessed interval is marked only on the margin, not drawn through. Rie swaps her oversized teacher clip for one the same size as the others.

exitImage.description: Jodi clips all three transparent sheets to the rehearsal stand at once. Rie reads the synthesis from the back row; the unwitnessed middle remains a bright gap instead of disappearing. A second back-row chair is pulled out for tomorrow, with Nanako's name on the visitor slip.

propCues.description: One option folds an account into the other two by dropping its vantage note. Compare that clause again; the blank middle span stays blank.

scenes.goal: Reach the point where a rehearsal line that spells out a private reason reads worse on stage than one that stops short and lets the gap carry the meaning.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Faced with a blank the audience might not understand, will the class explain it all the way down, or trust the omission to speak?
scenes.learnerNeed: A recognition check where the learner identifies the public line that preserves the deliberate blank without publishing a private reason.

intents: Arrive as a visitor, apologize lightly for being a little late, and ask only to watch the run-through from the side without stopping it.
Gently ask whether the private reason belongs on the stage at all — without correcting him — since the audience can feel the space was deliberate without being told why.
Read the trimmed line back and name what the omission is doing now: a line chosen and left off the page still counts as writing. This inverts her old habit of glossing everything so nothing was lost.
Read the draft closing note for the deliberately empty atlas section aloud, stacking on the full private reason so the audience will not be confused about why the space was left empty.

openingImage.description: The back-row chair from yesterday's overlay test is still pulled out. The classroom door opens on Henry's phrase 'the truth is.' Nanako stops there with her bag still on one shoulder. On the stage script, the next sentence says the earlier writer left town; unlike every other claim on the page, it has no source mark or permission note.

exitImage.description: Henry reads the shorter line from behind the tape and lets the marked three-second pause run. Nanako hears it from the back row without moving closer. The unpermitted clause is covered by a removable strip on the public copy, while the source draft remains intact and face-down.

propCues.description: Two versions sit side by side: one publishes the inferred reason, while the other stops at 「あえて空けてあります」. Compare what each version puts on stage.

scenes.goal: Let the learner decide how a contributor's own private reason stays off the public line without the line reading cold, sorting what is private register from what is public.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Can a stage line keep a reason private and still sound like the person who means it?
scenes.learnerNeed: A stance choice about whether to imply a kept-back reason or leave it fully off the page, holding the private/public register split.

intents: Worry that cutting his own reason will flatten the line into a plain report, so the audience won't feel why the work mattered.
Accept the cut without arguing it back, keeping only what he can hand to everyone and letting the rest stay his — the tool-first talker leaving a line understandable without over-explaining it.
Separate the private reason from the public line — the audience needs to feel the work is real, not to be told why; the reason can stay his, and the line still carries warmth without it.
Close cleanly, linking today's chosen omission back to words once left unfinished — some things stay between people on purpose, and that is authorship, not a failure to finish.

openingImage.description: The run-through has stopped at the last page, the line each contributor says in turn. Henry's own line still carries a clause about why the work matters to him, underlined once. In the margin, a small note in his hand reads 「これ要る?」.

exitImage.description: Two filenames appear on Henry's screen: STAGE and PRIVATE NOTES. The public line keeps its three-second pause; the personal clause remains untouched in the private copy. Nanako checks the train time, lifts one hand from the doorway, and is gone before Henry can reopen either file.

scenes.goal: Stop a first-page rehearsal at the sentence demanding one maker, and reach the point where the sentence itself becomes the thing to revise.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: When the spoken introduction leaves room for one name, does the class pick someone or question the line?
scenes.learnerNeed: A recognition check where the learner identifies the frame-shifting counterfactual that challenges the single-owner premise without blaming anyone in the room.

intents: Stop the rehearsal where its one-name sentence erases a different contributor whichever name she tries.
Catch the frame-shift and move from 'we have to name one' to questioning who decided that in the first place, opening the premise instead of defending it.
From the overlooked seat, question the premise rather than contradict anyone: use a counterfactual and premise-framing to ask whether finishing the atlas ever required a single owner at all.
Accept that the class has rejected the false premise and name the move precisely: he shifted the question from 'whose name' to 'is one name needed at all,' questioning the frame instead of a person.

openingImage.description: The projector holds on the rehearsal line 「このアトラスを作ったのは、＿＿です」. On the board, Sophie's first attempt at the blank has become a row of crossed-out names. The atlas lies open on the lectern. By the window, the chair no one thought to check is occupied after all; Peter watches with his notebook shut on one knee.

exitImage.description: Sophie strikes through the projected sentence, leaving every name on the board alone. Peter opens his notebook a finger's width, sees she has already begun the new line, and closes it again. 'Splendid,' he says, quietly enough that the projector fan nearly takes it.

propCues.description: The crossed-out names stay on the board. On the projector, a bracket now begins before 「このアトラスを作ったのは」 and ends after the blank. No name is circled; the sentence itself waits for another pass.

scenes.goal: Write and perform a replacement introduction that keeps contributions traceable without inventing one maker, then turn the rehearsal toward the futures waiting after the final night.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Will the new line still make sense from the back row when one early contribution remains unknown?
scenes.learnerNeed: A stance on how the spoken introduction names several kinds of contribution and preserves the part no source can assign.

intents: Offer a replacement stage line that follows routes, text, and photographs back as far as the sources allow, then stops honestly.
Run the revised line once more and hear it clear the old blank without hiding the unknown route.
Test the revised introduction from the back row, ask about the unnamed first route, and notice that an honest stop works better than a quick false answer.
Turn the rehearsal page and point to the next genuinely open question: what each person will do after the final public night.

openingImage.description: A strip of paper covers the old sentence on the rehearsal script. Sophie writes a new opening above it while Peter moves to the back row. Beside the lectern, three source cards wait under the headings 道, 文章, and 写真; one early route still has no name.

exitImage.description: Sophie clips the revised opening over the old one and runs it once without stopping. Peter turns the rehearsal page. The next card reads AFTER THIS NIGHT; Alex's name sits beneath it with no arrow, date, or destination. A cafe receipt is tucked under the corner for tomorrow.

scenes.goal: Meet Alex delivering the biggest news of the term in the flattest register in the room, and let the class refuse to let the send-off slide past without turning his leaving into a brave act.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: When the biggest fact lands in the calmest clause, will the room catch it and mark it on his terms?
scenes.learnerNeed: A stance on how to meet a flat, enormous announcement — naming the load-bearing clause the calm was hiding, and keeping the send-off from inflating.

intents: Deliver the term's biggest news in the flattest possible register, letting the load-bearing clause — next month, and already decided — land the calmest of all.
Under attention his voice narrows rather than opens — accept a send-off only if it stays small, and name the real uncertainty plainly without dramatizing it.
Accept a small send-off on plain terms, and refuse in advance to be made the one who did the brave thing.
Refuse to let the biggest clause pass flat — catch what he under-stressed, name it back, and ask, leaving him room to decline, to mark the leaving properly.

openingImage.description: The cafe receipt from yesterday's rehearsal sits under Aakash's phone, beside the card marked AFTER THIS NIGHT. Before Alex has finished taking off his jacket, the phone already shows a draft send-off poll: dinner, camera walk, or a full Saturday route. Alex reads all three options and says the part Aakash has got ahead of.

exitImage.description: Aakash deletes the three-option draft and sends a two-choice poll: usual cafe, or no separate event. Phones light around the table. Alex votes for the cafe, then turns his screen face-down before anyone can add a speech field.

scenes.goal: Let the class lay its different futures — leaving, staying, undecided — side by side, and hold them without ranking any above the others.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: When one person's 'someday in Japan' finally comes true, does the room rank it above the ones still open?
scenes.learnerNeed: A recognition check where the learner identifies the line that keeps each future in its honest modality without ranking them.

intents: Put his own future on the table as a genuine maybe — the solo camera road-trip — and hold it beside Alex's decided move without ranking either.
Show the reflex-organizer sitting with an open plan — keep the send-off small as Alex asked, and let his own trip stay undecided instead of accelerating it into an event.
Return remotely after a long absence without apology theatre, notice the three different futures already in the thread, and add her own concrete place in them.
Invite anyone whose study has lapsed to join her own small restart, with a concrete twenty-minute plan and an explicit no-reply easy-out.
Land the term's drifting 'someday, for work' on himself as payoff, reject the courage headline again, and bring the room back to his small cafe poll.

openingImage.description: The group chat fills with half-plans: one person's 'someday, for work,' another's 'maybe never,' a third's 'not decided.' After the thread goes quiet, a message from Mira appears beneath them under her plain nameplate.

exitImage.description: Alex's cafe vote remains the only mark on the send-off poll. Mira's twenty-minute review invitation sits below it with no reply required. Aakash closes the route-planning tab without booking anything, and the cafe receipt pins the phones in place when the door opens.

propCues.description: The three futures sit on cards at the same height: leaving, staying, undecided. The learner checks each written update against the thread: a decided time for Alex, an uncertainty marker for Aakash, and both staying and restarting language for Mira.

scenes.goal: Reach the moment the class stops trying to fill the withdrawn block and reframes the job as holding its place without showing it, and Stasi marks that place with a plain tab.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Faced with a blank that reads like a mistake, will the class fill the gap or design a mark that keeps it open on purpose?
scenes.learnerNeed: A stance on a plan that preserves a withheld place instead of restoring its content.

intents: Name the plain problem: the blank reads like a dropped stitch and they can't restore what was removed, so the real task is to build an absence that doesn't look like a gap.

Pay off the paper-cat: set a plain new marker in the withheld block's place and name the reversal. The old cat pointed at the clue; this one shows nothing and only keeps a place that must not be filled.

Reframe it from restoration to framing: the question is what to keep out of frame. Use the subtitle logic that a part you chose not to show stays truer unshown. Point at the room; don't open the door.

openingImage.description: Rain runs down the tall library windows. The near-final public panel lies flat across the long table, its blocks of caption set in reading order. One block is a bare rectangle of card where a withdrawn passage used to sit. Jenny has already re-blocked the panel from the back bench so the empty block falls where the layout can carry it, then gone back to her own work. Tom's old paper cat sits in an open box at the table's edge.

exitImage.description: Stasi lowers the matte grey bar by two millimetres and walks back to Jenny's bench. From there the eye lands on the caption's first verb, not the white block. Jenny gives one small nod and returns to her work; the measurement is written on the production copy.

scenes.goal: Turn the constraint into the final revised caption line: vivid, restoring nothing withdrawn, keeping the marker's place. The learner identifies the bounded revision from three visible options.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Can a line be cut down under a hard constraint and come out sharper instead of plainer?
scenes.learnerNeed: A recognition check where the learner identifies the vivid bounded line that restores no withdrawn detail.

intents: Use her ear as the accuracy tool: read the line aloud like a song, notice the clause that feels too good, and propose dropping it to test whether the line stands on its own or was leaning on the withdrawn certainty.
Sign off by singing the finished line through once: nothing drops, it stands all the way, and it can go out.
Lock the three plain editing conditions (keep the vividness, put nothing withdrawn back, keep the marker's place), then hand the learner a choice among visible revisions with an easy way to decline.
Land the arc: the constrained line came out sharper, not smaller. It reached this shape because they could not restore or fill, and it kept every bit of the vividness while letting no lie in.
Close her framing arc: what they chose not to show stays unshown to the end, and the piece is finished and honest. Filling it without showing it is the hardest thing to pull off, and it worked.

openingImage.description: On the board, the draft is pinned up large: 「この道は、戻らなかった人の願いを受け継ぎ、今夜も灯る。」 The middle clause leans on the very detail the class agreed to withhold. Beneath it, the bounded candidate is written once: 「この道は、今夜も静かに灯る。」 The grey marker stays in its block below both lines.

exitImage.description: Stasi steps back two metres, Ruparna checks the crop from the side, and Xingyu reads the finished caption once. Tom closes the paper cat in its box and slides the grey marker across the table. Each person leaves one tested action behind before the panel goes into its rain cover.

propCues.description: Compare the middle clauses again. The candidate 「この道は、今夜も静かに灯る。」 keeps the visible image without putting the withdrawn claim back on the wall.

title.ja: いなくても、回るように

scenes.goal: Meet Henry mid-rehearsal handing over a tested, documented projection setup and reach the point where it must become someone else's to run.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Can a setup that only its builder understands be handed over so it runs without him in the room?
scenes.learnerNeed: A run-sheet that turns a private, tested setup into instructions another person can follow under uncertainty.

intents: Present the tested, documented projection setup and say plainly that he wants it to run on the night without him, qualifying his own certainty late.
Credit Angel's off-scene work making the plan readable to anyone, and name what it takes for a setup to keep running when its builder is gone.
Include the one connector he was famous for forgetting, taped to the box, and name honestly that this time it goes over attached.
Offer his own already-tested fix for the room, and this time hand it to someone else to run instead of owning it, leaving the fan behind for the next class.

openingImage.description: The projector lights before Henry reaches the front desk. Shaun is already on cue two, following the labelled run-sheet with the adapter taped beside it. Christian's fan turns on low at the back of the room. Henry stops in the aisle with the equipment box still in his hands.

exitImage.description: The box now carries a label anyone could read, the adapter cable taped to its side under the words for it. The fan sits apart with a note that it stays for the next class. The run-sheet ends on a line addressed to whoever runs it, not to Henry.

propCues.description: The run-sheet is laid open to two lines: a pre-set step and the branch that follows when the light stays dark. Only the line that another person could not yet follow comes back for a second pass; the parts that already read clearly stay put.

scenes.goal: Let the class rehearse the goodbye alongside the event and settle how Henry hands the setup over to be run without him.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Is a handoff a set of steps to follow exactly, or a thing given over for the next person to change?
scenes.learnerNeed: A stance choice about whether the run-sheet binds the next runner to it or is handed over as theirs to adjust.

intents: Say out loud that he will not be in the room on the night and ask the class to run the setup themselves, with a contact left for anything unexpected.
Make the honorific request to run it, and admit that at this point the setup already belongs to the class more than to him — support given before it is called that.
Give the one bounded register-check that is his to give — the reception sign should read to guests, not to the class — and mark that this is the extent of his part.
Accept the setup and take on the one bounded part that is his, without reaching for anything larger.

openingImage.description: Shaun calls cue three and the transparent accounts appear one at a time. Henry stays in the back row, the equipment box under his chair. At cue four, Shaun glances once at the run-sheet, changes the reception slide, and continues without looking toward Henry.

exitImage.description: Shaun powers the projector down, waits for the fan to stop, then starts cue one again from a dark screen. Henry remains in the back row with empty hands. The fan's note stays clipped for the next class; the unlabelled recorder is lifted once, held, and set down again.

scenes.goal: Present the atlas to a mixed public and repair, out loud, a live misunderstanding the moment it happens.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: When the answer starts to run ahead of the question in front of an audience, does the panel push on, or stop and hear it again?
scenes.learnerNeed: A way to catch that a question was misheard, hold the room through the pause, and re-open it so the answer can start clean.

intents: Relay the audience question to the panel and start answering it — but answer the version the panel thinks it heard (who made the atlas) rather than the one that was asked.
Take Mika's stop and make it graceful in public — tell the room openly that the panel may have misheard, and invite the asker to say it once more without anyone losing face.
Stop the panel before it answers the wrong question, ask the asker to repeat, and name the mismatch plainly — then stay in the pause instead of stepping back.

openingImage.description: Paper lanterns cross the courtyard for the public evening. Folding chairs face the atlas panels; the audience runs from fluent to two-lessons-in. A question has just come up from the third row and the whole panel has turned to take it. Rie stands at the back by the tea, nowhere near the microphone.
