exitImage.description: The question is back on the courtyard, this time the way it was meant: who has kept the atlas going. Not who made it. A harder question, and an honest one, and now the panel has room to answer instead of racing past it.

propCues.description: In the third row the person who asked tilts their head a fraction; that isn't quite what they said. Off to one side Xingyu lets a single low note hang under her breath, the way she marks a beat. Mika, who has not spoken all evening, lifts one finger — wait — and counts the pause before the panel commits.
Only the one phrase comes again, slower: the asker repeats it, and this time the room hears the difference between 作った and 守ってきた. Nobody hurries to fill the gap while it lands.

scenes.goal: Answer the re-heard question in public only to the level the record supports, keeping heard, inferred, and not-yet-sayable plainly apart.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Under an audience's eyes, does the class fill the unknown to sound finished, or leave it standing where everyone can see it?
scenes.learnerNeed: A public stance that states what was heard and what was inferred without letting the part it cannot establish sound like a failure.

intents: Tell the audience plainly that the panel will answer to the level the record supports and no further — set the honest terms out loud before answering.
Close the evening as a host who no longer needs a hidden reveal — thank the room, and let the part they couldn't answer stand as something they showed on purpose, not something to apologize away.

Put the actual split into words for the room — one thing heard and confirmed, one thing inferred, one thing that cannot be established — and refuse to let the empty third column sound like a shortfall.
Name, quietly and only to the class, that the stop worked because the room has learned to use his pause on purpose — drop the observation and, this time, stay in it instead of retreating.
Close the public part with a single clear invitation to the after-gathering — one real opening, an easy way to decline — and, this time, not branch it into a dozen options.

openingImage.description: Ruparna turns the board toward the courtyard. Its three columns now hold three source cards: Rie's bounded memory, the former learner's letter, and the later contribution record. A final row, uninterrupted chain of stewardship, has no supporting card.

exitImage.description: At the reception table Robert catches a tray mix-up, names the correct one once, and moves no other plate. Any first-hand audience note goes into a sealed follow-up envelope with a name and permission choice, not onto the live board. Rie's tea remains untouched at the back, still warm; Mika stays beside Francis as the microphone is switched off.

scenes.goal: Reach the point where Rie has confirmed what she did and did not make, named the ordinary mechanism, and the class must state a conclusion that goes no further than the record.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Faced with an atlas that no one fully authored, will the class invent an owner to finish it or conclude only as far as the record honestly reaches?
scenes.learnerNeed: A final synthesis that attributes what the record supports and marks the rest as unknown, using calibrated hedges and embedded quotation.

intents: Confirm plainly what she personally did, distinguish it from the earlier learner's attributed statement and the later contribution records, and state that neither the first route nor a complete sequence can be verified.

Name the ordinary mechanism behind the atlas's apparent responsiveness — Angel and Henry's projection chain, the paper itself plain — so nothing mysterious is left to explain, echo the very first evening, and propose that they conclude the provenance only as far as the record actually reaches.

Accept the synthesis and close her part of the atlas without signing what she did not do — the template is hers, the routes belong to many hands, some marks to no one she can name — and mark that limit as the honest end rather than a failure.

Report what the physical marks let him establish and, for the first time, name the exact point where reading stops: he can order some hands by their brush habit but cannot assign every one — the characters are easy, the history is not.

openingImage.description: The classroom is set for a small public inquiry: a few visitors' chairs, the finished lantern-atlas hung on the back wall, and the projection cart pushed dark against the side. On a long desk lie the provenance records and Sophie's colour-coded evidence map, one cell left as a labelled blank. Rie stands beside the atlas's oldest, near-empty layer, a cup of tea going cold at her elbow.

exitImage.description: Rie signs beside the handoff of the blank backing sheet and nowhere else. The letter writer's attributed statement and the later contribution record keep their own source lines; first route and complete sequence remain marked unverified. She caps the pen. The tea at her elbow has gone cold, untouched.

propCues.description: The synthesis is split into two columns on the record: what the evidence supports and what it does not reach. Only the part that overran the evidence — a claim written a step past what the record holds — returns for another pass; the attributions that already sat inside the evidence stay written.

scenes.goal: Let the class conclude the provenance only as far as the material evidence reaches, keeping a labelled blank instead of an invented owner, and close the atlas on those terms.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Can a record that stops exactly where the evidence stops — blank cell and all — count as more finished than one filled in to look complete?
scenes.learnerNeed: A stance on whether the record should conclude to a single owner or hold each account only as far as the evidence licenses.

intents: Turn from her own attribution to the record's, and hand the material reading to Rose — ask plainly what the physical evidence does and does not let them claim.
Give the record a plain cross-reference, keep her own signature bounded to the handoff she remembers, and ask the class to perform the final physical closure with her.

State what the material evidence can and cannot license — the paper, ink, and wear prove the page passed through several classes, but proving what a thing is made of is not proving whose story it is — and conclude only as far as the evidence reaches.
Turn her material finding into a bounded action: colour and sign the material row while refusing to colour the attribution row that her samples cannot support.

openingImage.description: The class gathers at the long desk where Sophie's evidence map lies open beside the old number notebook. Every cell carries a colour: one for what the record establishes, one for what is only inferred, one left deliberately blank and labelled 'we don't know this yet.' Rose stands over it with two ink samples in her hand.

exitImage.description: The two people nearest the wall lift the atlas free while Rie keeps the signed record from sliding. One lowers the cover; the other closes the last latch. The name field reads only 'see contribution record.' Rose returns the extra pen beside the map. Rie's cold tea remains at the desk's edge.

scenes.goal: Turn from the latched atlas to a separate graduation sheet, and make its optional one-contribution terms concrete before anyone writes.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Now that the atlas is closed, what does the class leave for whoever comes next, and on whose terms?
scenes.learnerNeed: A stance on how to approach writing a bounded final page when every tone is accepted and no one is assigned to fill it.

intents: Put away the marking pen, identify the four usable tones, and set the bounded permission plainly: leave one thing if wanted, or pass the pen on.
Make non-grading visible by keeping the red pen in the drawer, accept writing, drawing, or sound, and use Robert's dishes for a small practical warning.
Test the just-finished scarf against a chair, decide to leave both for the next arrival, and make the handoff practical rather than ceremonial.
Show his still-unsubmitted December exam form, distinguish indecision from a false claim of action, and choose to take the live question home with him.

openingImage.description: The classroom door opens onto a loose ring of chairs. The atlas is shut in its case on the back table; beside it, Shaun has coiled the projection cable next to Henry's seven-cue run-sheet. A separate sheet in the middle is held against the summer breeze by four cards: THANKS, ADVICE, QUESTION, MARK. Someone has placed a red pen beside Rie's fresh tea. She picks up the pen first and looks around.

exitImage.description: Jenny moves the sheet and its four cards into the middle of the ring, then takes the blue pen around herself. Before Rie can follow, Jenny nudges the steaming cup into the hand Rie has left empty. Rie catches it with both hands and stays in her chair.

scenes.goal: Let the learner leave one bounded contribution in a chosen tone, establish the sheet's ordinary unwired state, and complete the room-closing handoff from Henry to Shaun.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: What does the learner choose to leave, and will Rie actually stay seated while Shaun performs the last cue?
scenes.learnerNeed: An integrated N1 production: author one bounded final contribution in a chosen tone under the class's permission terms.

intents: Set the blue pen and recorder within reach, point to the coiled projection cable as physical proof that the sheet is unwired, and return the learner to one chosen card.
Accept the contribution without reading or correcting it, ask Shaun to perform the final lock-up cue, and choose the still-steaming tea as her own last action.

openingImage.description: The sheet makes one slow circuit. Robert tapes 'ask before choosing the dish' beside a one-place setting. Felix notes the time beside a small shape at the window and adds a question mark instead of a species name. Stasi draws the red pen disappearing into Rie's drawer. Jodi props the same station photograph between two captions and keeps both. Shaun checks the door key against cue seven on Henry's run-sheet. The other farewells go into the journal, not into speeches.

exitImage.description: Shaun reads cue seven once, checks the windows, turns off the projector-cart switch that is already dark, and works the door latch. At its click Rie starts to rise, then settles back and drinks. The tea is still warm. Jenny's scarf clears the floor on the chair kept for the next arrival; Peter's form is back in his bag. The atlas case stays latched. On the separate sheet, the learner's one contribution remains exactly as they left it.

propCues.description: Only the part that ran long comes back. The learner sets down everything but the one thing they meant — keeping a single stitch and letting the rest drop. What's already on the page stays where it is.

Overnight the atlas's first route has been covered end to end in tiny hand-drawn marks: doubled strokes, small hooks, single and double circles. It is dense, even, and clearly a system. A folded slip in the corner is labelled KEY in the same unreadable hand.
One plain hiragana word — えき — now sits among Henry's dense marks, the first point on the route anyone can find. His cipher is untouched all around it; only one gap has been made legible.
Only the plain-kana label and its reason clause return for another try. Henry's dense marks around the point stay exactly where they were — editing the point never rubs out his system.

Beside the one readable point sits Henry's pen case, each pen tagged in his own marks, and a stack of blank label cards. He turns a fresh card over and half-reaches to draw the next point in cipher again.

The route now carries plain hiragana names along its line, and Henry's cipher is folded into a small labelled key in the corner. Anyone entering the room can read the route; nothing of the system has been thrown away.

Rain sheets past the station exit. A route map glows on the wet glass, every turn tagged with an automatic place-name label. A puddle throws the labels back in neon — the whole street reads like a record sleeve. Aakash arrives a few minutes late, waving the class over.
A single place-name label re-inks itself over the corner shop. The rest of the route is still blank, but it has its first named point again — and it came from a question, not the map.

Every automatic place-name label peels off the map at once and dissolves into the rain. The route is still there — the crossing, the corner, the shop — but nothing is named. Aakash's pointing finger stops in mid-air over a blank tag.

Rie uncaps a marker to write どこ on the blank tag; it runs dry precisely on the last stroke of こ. She holds up the dead marker, unbothered, and nods the learner toward the corner instead — the question will have to be spoken, not written.
The person-question fades out. Only the place-question frame stays lit — the blank corner tag and one particle slot — for another try. No English answer appears before the learner commits.
Aakash lowers his pointing hand. For once he isn't adding the next turn. The one recovered label holds on the corner; the rest of the street waits, unnamed, in the rain.

The single recovered label holds steady on the corner. The rest of the street stays unnamed — but now the class knows the route isn't in the labels; it's in the asking. Aakash pockets his pointing hand and, for once, waits.
A new point on the atlas route stays shut behind a closed gate. Under the class's overlapping voices, a soft chime repeats at the same faint interval, over and over, unanswered.
The route point lights, faintly, exactly on the chime's beat. The passage behind the gate is open now, and two overlapping voices can be heard inside it.
The class leans in and calls out louder, all at once, trying to force the point open. The gate does not move. The chime keeps its interval as if the shouting were not there.
Only the single interval that was missed replays, slowed, with a count marked over the pause. The rest of the passage stays where the learner left it; no English answer appears first.
Inside the passage, two recorded voices overlap. Each names an item; each says one is theirs. A single card label carries a kanji the atlas has left unread.
A small marker settles on the atlas at the opened point: not a lantern, just a mark that means listen. It keeps a steady, quiet beat while the route runs on past it.

Tom clears the front desk and lays out an oversized card game. Five big katakana cards stand in a row, three round tokens beside them. One card towers over the rest, hand-labelled ボス. On the battered game box, a small photo sticker of a dog is captioned チェスナットさん. Clipped to the smallest, plainest card at the edge is a folded paper cat, easy to miss.
The ボス card stands drawn and enormous at the centre, and the game sits stalled around it. At the edge of the table, unmoved, the folded paper cat still marks the smallest, plainest card.

Only the card that was misread turns back face up on its own; the cards already read correctly stay where the learner placed them. No English gloss appears — just the katakana, a little larger, waiting to be read again.

The class has crowded in around the giant ボス card, arguing about how to beat it. At the edge of the table, the small card with the folded paper cat sits untouched, its plain katakana facing up and unread.

The giant ボス card is set aside, face down. In the middle of the table sits the small card reading ネコ, face up, the folded paper cat resting on top of it. On the game box, the little dog sticker captioned チェスナットさん watches over the whole thing.
The cafe's corner table already has glasses and a jug set out, poured before anyone agreed to anything. A notepad waits in the middle under Sam's pen.

The extra branches fold away, leaving a single card with a time slot and an activity slot. Only the phrasing chunk that went missing — the time range or the invitation ending — returns for another try; the chosen day and activity stay put.
The notepad fills with branching options — days, dishes, drinks, tennis-first-or-after — arrows crossing arrows. The poured drinks sit untouched, going flat. Nobody at the table answers.
On the cleared notepad, one line remains: Saturday, from six, okonomiyaki. Every other branch has been set aside. The card can finally be answered.
One clear invitation, one honored answer. The Saturday card stays out on the table for whoever's free; the flat drinks are cleared and fresh ones poured for the people who are here now.

A paper curtain is strung across the back of the cafe with a hand-lettered sign: NO SPOILERS BEYOND THIS CURTAIN. A small round plush sits on the sill like a guard. Along the front tables, seat-cards mark how far each person has watched — 3話, 5話, 最終話 — no two the same. A manga volume lies face-down by a half-eaten plate; the host's hoodie carries a faint kitchen smell.

The paper curtain stays drawn across the back of the cafe. But now voices cross it in both directions — careful, past-tense, none of them carrying the thing behind it. The plush on the sill has not had to move.

By the counter, a cup of tea sits where Rie set it down an hour ago, a thin skin cooling on its surface. She is three tables away, restacking chairs and steering two latecomers to seats, and has not come back to it. Francis, mid-sentence, notices the cup before anyone else does.

Two slots are set out side by side: a past-tense impression slot and a floor-opening question slot. Only the slot that leaked toward the reveal returns for another try; the safe half the learner already landed stays put.

Someone has taped a SAFE WORDS list to the wall: gentle stand-ins for the reveal — 「例の人」, 「例のこと」, 「アレ」. Under the curtain, the three seat-cards still mark three different stopping points. The list looks careful. It also looks like a treasure map.

A phone buzzes face-up on the table — a shift reminder lights the screen. Francis glances at it, turns it face-down without reading past the first line, and looks back up at the room. Along the wall the seat-cards begin to move: everyone marking where they are, no two the same, and not one of them saying what's behind the curtain.

A cramped ramen counter before class. The whole wall is a hand-brushed menu: black characters on cream paper, no photos, no prices in numerals anyone can find fast. Steam curls up past the last empty stools.

The wall menu no longer reads as a solid block. The 肉 dishes sit in one column, the 魚 and 野菜 dishes in another, and the meat-free bowl the learner picked out is circled in chalk. The steam behind the counter thickens as an order is called back.

One dish name lifts off the wall and splits into its left and right parts, side by side. Only the piece that went unread returns for another try; the parts already decoded stay in place, and the counter phrase waits underneath.
Everyone has claimed a stool along the counter. One dish name near the bottom of the wall is still unread, and Shin taps it with the end of his pencil instead of saying it.

Bowls land along the counter, one to each stool. Robert's meat-free bowl sits among them, no different to look at. Behind the diners the wall menu stays legible now — two columns, one circled line — the way Shin left it.

A stack of old photographs goes hand to hand around the table for captioning. One stops in front of the class: a Tokyo street corner, a small shopfront on the left, the print soft at the edges. A blank caption slip waits beneath it.

The photo now carries two caption slips at once — one in the past tense, one in the present — pinned side by side. Neither is crossed out. The corner in the picture stays exactly as half-there as it always was.

The past slip and the present slip are set side by side beneath the photo. Only the tense or the reason that went missing returns for another try; the caption already written stays in place, uncrossed.
The photo rests under the desk lamp with both captions kept. Jodi looks at it for a moment longer than the task needs, the way you look at a place rather than a picture.

The photo is pinned to the working atlas with both captions beneath it, shifted just far enough that the route line remains visible. Bread smell belongs to the past slip; the convenience-store light belongs to the present one. Neither is crossed out.
location:courtyard at evening

In the courtyard, a brass weather-lantern sits on a bench. Beside it a stack of numbered instruction cards is pinned in order under a small clip; an electric desk fan hums at the end of the bench, and a phone glows nearby with a homework tab already open.
The cloud runs its parts in sequence, one glow after another. One last card is still in Christian's hand, not yet pinned; he turns it over but does not add it to the row.

A gust crosses the courtyard and lifts the clip. The cards spin down shuffled, their numbers no longer in a row. On the lantern, every part of the cloud lights at once — a flat white glare instead of a sequence.
The re-laid cards stay where the learner placed them. Only the one card that landed out of sequence lifts back out for another try, its reason line shown blank beside it.
location:courtyard at evening

Christian sits on the bench with the last card still in his hand. The fan hums beside him; a small recorder is out on the bench too, and nobody says anything about it. He looks from the card to the people around the lantern.

The cloud runs its whole sequence, one glow after another, with Christian's hands off it. The last card passes from person to person around the lantern. The fan hums on the bench; the recorder is still there, unremarked.

The exhibition street after the storm: every signpost stands bare, its route plate torn away. Puddles hold the last of the wind. One figure walks up without hurrying, a folded paper map in his coat pocket.
A thin route line joins the rebuilt steps along the street — and runs straight into a corner where standing water fills the underpass. The line stops at the water's edge.
The steps already placed stay pinned along the street. Only the one connector that slipped out of order returns for another attempt.
The rebuilt route ends at the flooded underpass. Water sits across the whole corner. A second figure comes up the street from the far side, already gesturing past the water toward a narrow side lane.
The route line redraws itself: it turns at the bakery, runs down the side lane, and ends at a lit doorway. The old flooded corner is simply left off the map, no longer a problem to solve.

The cafe counter is lined with covered dishes and a row of small serving cards, each meant to say what the dish is, how many there are, and when it goes out. Above the counter the class's paper atlas waits with one unlit route point at its edge.
Plated to the count the room agreed on, one warm course is ready to go round. Above the counter, the single route point at the atlas's edge begins, faintly, to glow. Every other route stays blank.

One by one the serving cards go blank — every label, every count, every order-arrow wiped away. Jenny, a half-finished scarf still looped over one wrist, coaxes one tangled serving-string back into place, then looks up at the covered dishes waiting without a single label.
One covered dish is set forward on its own beside an empty count-slot. Only the single item that went uncounted returns for another try; the parts already described and counted stay in place.

The one warm course leaves the counter and starts round the table. On the atlas the single lit route point holds steady while the rest of the map stays dark. Jenny watches it move, the half-finished scarf resting now against her arm.

The one course has gone all the way round the table. The single lit route holds on the atlas; the rest of the map is still blank. The serving cards now lie within everyone's reach. In Jenny's lap, one stitch returns to the half-finished scarf.
The cafe's long table is set not with food but with ordered cards: soup, salad, pasta, each pinned to the next with a hand-drawn arrow. Steam waits behind the counter.
Robert takes down the extra cards. One dish remains on the table, with no arrow after it. The gap is simply left.
A delivery crate is short one box. The card that says 'salad' no longer has anything behind its arrow. The chain now points at nothing.
The two remaining cards are set side by side. Only the comparison phrase that went missing returns for another try; the earlier decision stays.
For the first time all evening Robert sits down instead of moving between cards. He turns the one remaining card face up and leaves it.
One dish goes round the table and is enough. The empty arrow-space stays on the card, no longer a problem to solve.
On the rebuilt map, one route caption reads 「この灯りは一時間◯三回つきます」 with the particle slot left open. Two classmates have penciled different answers over it: に and で. Neither has been erased.

Sophie leaves the caption's particle slot open and lays a small notebook beside the map. On its first page the number three is written twice — once under a per-hour card, once under a one-observed-hour card.
The two contexts are set out side by side: a per-hour rhythm card and a single-observed-hour card. Only the context that went unmatched returns for another try; the matched one stays put.

The small notebook lies open between Sophie and Rose. It is ruled into two columns: one headed for a claim, one headed for the context it was counted in. Sophie uncaps a blue pen and a green one; the claim column is still empty.

The caption keeps its open slot with a small mark pointing off the page. Beside the map the notebook stays open, the number three recorded twice in blue and green, each under its own context. Nothing is crossed out.

Three katakana cards are taped across the board in a row: ライト, ルート, and a third whose middle is left blank. Xingyu taps the desk in time and hums a tune that stumbles on a small gap right at the third card.
The third card now reads full, and Xingyu taps four beats where he had been tapping three. The tune keeps its bounce; only the stumble is gone.
Half the room is already humming it back — and everyone hums the gap too, landing on the same little silence where the beat should be. The flaw is the part that stuck.
The third card is held up with its blank still open, and Xingyu sings only the short word again, slower. Just the one dropped sound waits for another try; the rest of the chant stays as it was.
Xingyu hums the whole chant through once, clean now. Tom is up on the balls of his feet, plainly itching to turn it into a contest again.
The room runs the chant once through: three full words, and on the fourth beat that used to be a hole, everyone claps together. The gap is kept on purpose now.

The rebuilt route glows across the wall, flickering at one corner. The paper map on the table beneath it is blank; the light is the only copy. Angel stands at the console with a printed step-card, checking it line by line.
No one is looking at the wall anymore. Chairs shift away from the dark projection and into a loose circle. The blank paper map is passed to the middle.

The reset runs exactly as written. The flicker stops — and so does everything else. The route, every label, drains off the wall. The paper underneath stays blank. The room's only copy of the map was the light.
The wall stays dark. No one is at the console. Henry sits in the circle with the blank paper map and a pen — not the keyboard — turning it so everyone can reach it.

The route comes back across the blank paper map, drawn from spoken pieces in several different hands. The wall stays dark. The class is holding the map now, not the screen; Rie signs off only the seams.
The segments already taught back stay on the paper. Only the one cause-and-segment that did not land clearly returns for another try; the joins Rie is watching hold.
The library's reading table holds five route cards in a row, each stamped with a printed number. A small folded paper cat sits on one of them, facing the others. The numbers do not run left to right.
One by one the cards are drawn into the sequence the cat has been sitting through. The printed numbers stay stamped where they are, ignored. A thin trail is now visible in the placement itself.

Someone turns the cards to read the stamped numbers aloud: two, then five, then one. The printed order contradicts itself, and no card can be trusted by its own label. The class stalls over which card really comes first.
The marked card is lifted a little clear of the row so only it and the cat are in view. Just the relative-clause phrasing that slipped returns for another attempt; the count of cards stays as it was.

Felix lines up where the cat has sat on each past evening. The marks fall into one unbroken line across the cards — a walkway the cat has been pacing while the labels stayed wrong. He stops moving and just looks at it.
The class reads the five cards aloud in the cat's order and the route holds. The paper cat is set on the last card in the line, facing the empty table, ready to move again the next evening.

The classroom's side board has become a small museum: rows of hand-drawn kanji memory cards pinned in a grid, each with its own picture. In front of one card — 味, drawn as a wide-open mouth clamped over a leafy branch — a small knot of people has gathered. The projector shows an empty flashcard shell, waiting to be filled.
Only the sentence about the button and the changed part returns for another pass. The picture and the earlier welcome stay exactly where they were.

On the projector the two shapes sit side by side, 木 and 未, with the extra top stroke of 未 circled. Below them the empty program shell now shows a single labelled control: a part button marked ぶひん, waiting for what it should reveal.

On the projector the revised card draft has appeared: the same wide-open mouth, but now clamped over a hard green fruit, with 未 labelled beside it and the ぶひん button sitting underneath, ready to press.

The revised card goes back on the wall as the museum's first finished piece — the mouth still mid-bite, 未 in the corner, the ぶひん button glowing on the projector beside it. The wrong stroke is gone; the joke is not.

The library's back corner is dark except for a paused frame on the wall screen: a kitchen, a bowl, a person half-turned toward a window. A subtitle line sits ready under it. Ruparna stands beside the screen, not the switch.

Two columns stand on the whiteboard: one of lines the class actually caught, one of what it read in. Neither column pretends to be the other. The blank subtitle bar still glows under the paused frame.

The clip starts. The subtitle line stutters into broken glyphs, then goes blank and stays blank. The picture and the voices keep running with nothing written under them. Two people near the front shift in their seats.

Only the one moment that stayed unclear is scrubbed back and played again, a little slower. The heard-and-inferred columns already filled in stay on the whiteboard; just the ambiguous line waits for another read.
The clip pauses on the last frame. Sophie caps the marker and steps back so the two columns are both readable. The heard column is longer than the seats near the front expected.
The blank subtitle bar stays blank under the last frame. A small tag beside it reads 'unconfirmed'. Under the tag, Ruparna writes one short note: 「次の場面へ」.

The atlas backing panel lies flat on the long classroom table, its old pencil route half rubbed away. Three blank index cards wait along it. Rose crouches to table height, reading the paper's wear before anyone's writing.
The three cards sit in a numbered row along the backing, each route intact. The hovering eraser is capped and set down. The old fold-crease still shows underneath them all.
Three cards now sit along the backing, each tracing the same stretch a different way. A pencil eraser hovers over two of them, ready to make the map agree with itself.
The two diverging cards are set square against Alex's sequence. Only the comparison phrase that slipped comes back for another pass; the accounts already counted stay where they are.
The backing stands upright now, the three cards clipped along the route line. A printed exhibition label waits beside it with one narrow slot marked 'the route'.

The finished label carries the shared stretch as one line and the diverging stretch marked as remembered several ways. Three faint routes stay on the backing, counted, none erased, the old fold-crease still visible beneath them.

One district of the projected classroom map has gone dark. The cards pinned along it are blank, and the class has crowded around a single chair, waiting for the one person who might remember the whole area. Peter sits apart at the edge of the room, watching.

One block of the map warms back to light. The card that was blank now carries a single line in the learner's hand. The rest of the district stays dark — but the chair in the middle is empty now; no one is waiting for a perfect memory anymore.

Someone takes the single chair and tries to recite the whole district from memory, shop by shop. Three shops in, the list runs dry. The blank cards stay blank. The room keeps its eyes on the chair, waiting for a better memory to arrive.
Only the question comes back for another pass — the classmate and their one remembered detail stay in place. The half-formed question is set down and picked up again, one word at a time.

Half the district is lit now, block by block, each card in a different hand. The class has stopped looking at the single chair and started looking at Peter, who has not moved from the edge of the room.

Card by card, the district comes back to light, each in a different hand. Peter stays at the edge where he began, but now the questions move out from him and the answers come back to the room. The single empty chair in the middle stays empty. No one sits in it.
The classroom board carries the rebuilt route as a row of dialogue cards, each pinned in order. A five-second game timer sits under them. One card near the middle is still blank, its slot unfilled.

The card that stood blank now holds two lines — one casual, one polite — with a small arrow between them. The other route cards stay in their formal register, unchanged. The game timer resets to zero.

A player reaches the keigo card and runs out of sentence before the timer runs out; the buzzer cuts in. As it does the door opens and Shaun slips in late, setting a flattened paper bag on the side table. The blank card is still blank.

The single blank card is split down the middle: the casual opening on one side, the polite reply on the other. Only the register that slipped is offered again; the choice of which line goes where stays.

The board now shows each route beat in two columns — casual and polite — with the once-blank card at the head of the row. Shaun stays near the door, the flattened pastry unwrapped on a napkin, watching the next round set up.

The next round starts with each card offering two registers and a small marker beside the once-blank slot for Shaun's signal. He stays by the door, calling out only when a line turns stiff. The blank space on the board is gone, filled not by one right answer but by a register chosen out loud each time.

A hand-drawn timeline runs across the cafe board: 作る → 食べる → お礼. Beside it hangs a clock. The kitchen behind the counter is still busy with someone else's order; the first step has not begun, and the last step is the one the group circled twice.
The board now reads お礼 first; 作る sits behind a small 「時間があれば」. The stove stays cold. Behind the counter, someone lays out a row of name cards for the thank-you round instead of plates.

The counter is not free yet, and the clock leaves less time than the three steps need. On the board the 作る arrow still points at an empty stove. The order that was meant to end in thanks now cannot even start.
The board is wiped to just two boxes, お礼 and 作る. Only the before/after word between them returns for another try; the decision to put thanks first stays.

The name cards lie in a row, one per friend at the table, each meant for a single line of thanks. A few are turned face up and spoken; most are still face down. The clock has crept close to the time Nanako has to leave.

The door closes. On the table the thank-you cards stay half turned, the spoken ones and the unspoken ones side by side. Nobody flips the rest over. The unfinished round is simply left, held over, not cleaned up.

At the counter a hand turns down the lamp over the table. The borrowed evening is nearly up. More than half the name cards are still face down when the room goes quiet, waiting on what the learner will do with the rest.
Nanako gathers her coat and stands by the door. The board still reads お礼 first, the stove still cold, the cards still half turned. Nothing has been cleared away.
location:courtyard at evening

The winter courtyard is strung for the exhibition. The lantern-atlas glows along every route but the last one, which stays black end to end. The class is packed around a projector cart at its base, feeding it cables. A phone propped against the cart has just connected to the shared call, its camera pointed at the dark route.

The cables go slack on the ground and the cart is rolled to one side. Someone lifts the phone from it and props it beside the first route card. The class turns from the machine to the map, spreading into a loose line along the dark route.
The cable is swapped. A second projector hums on. The brightness dial goes up. The final route stays exactly as black as before. Behind the fence, the first guests begin to line up.
location:courtyard at evening

Along the dark route, Stasi has laid the segment cards out in reading order, colour-edged so each hand-off is visible at a glance. Each person picks up the card in front of them. Mira's voice comes from the phone beside the first card. The route waits, unlit.

As the finished route settles into a steady glow, one panel in the atlas backing catches the light from behind — a line of older handwriting the projection never threw onto the wall, with no name in the field beside it. Rose, gathering the spare cables at the back, stops with her hand flat against it.

Ruparna walks the route once, tracing it with a fingertip and setting a small chalk tick at each corner where a voice must breathe so the next one does not collide with it. The order is agreed; only the timing between voices is still loose.
The route holds up to the corner where two voices overlapped. Only that single hand-off is taken again on the same agreed order; the segments already lit stay lit while the learner re-times the pass.

The classroom the day after the first exhibition. The booth banner lies folded over a desk. In the corner of the whiteboard, last term's small tag still hangs — 「聞こえた／未確認 — 約7割」. Ruparna, leaning by the door, taps it once and says nothing. Beneath it Francis has written a single line: 「……けっこうです」, the last thing one visitor said on the way out.

Three readings now stand side by side on the board — 褒め, ためらい, お断り — each with the evidence that fed it: the words, the length of the pause, the fall of the voice. None is crossed out. The visitor's line stays written exactly as it was said.

Three blank reading-cards are set out — 褒め / ためらい / お断り. Only the reading that went untagged returns for another pass, its evidence line still empty; the readings already backed by the words, the pause, or the tone stay where they are.
The three readings are still on the board. Peter has turned up in the seat by the side wall that nobody had thought to check, notebook already open. The visitor's line waits below, unrounded.

The record now reads the phrase verbatim — 「……けっこうです」, pause and all — with three intents tagged beneath it as separate inferences. Beside it the old 約7割 tag has a line added: 全部聞こえても、全部は分からない. Nothing has been smoothed into a compliment; the visitor's words stay in the visitor's register.
location:library at evening/spring-evening

In the library, the exhibition atlas lies face-down on the worktable, its cloth backing peeled back at one corner. On the old paper underneath, a single caption is written in faded ink — a complete sentence — and above it, where a signature line would sit, there is nothing. Rose's fingers rest at the peeled corner. In the margin beside the caption, Shin has already penciled the reading over every character; the author line stays blank.

The caption lies face-up with its author line still blank. Beside it, a description card now reads what the sentence is and that its writer is unknown — no name invented, no owner assigned. Shin's full reading sits in the margin, every character legible, the author still nobody.

Two description cards are set out side by side: one that assigns a maker — 『◯◯によって書かれた』 with the name space still empty — and one that nominalizes the content and states plainly that the author is unknown. Only the card that reached past the evidence into naming returns for another try; the honest description stays where it is.
location:library at evening/spring-evening

On the worktable, the atlas backing lies open beside the described caption. A fresh record sheet is ruled with two headings: one for what the caption is, one for where it came from. The what-heading has the sentence under it already. The source line is still empty.

The caption stays face-up, its author line blank on purpose. The record sheet reads what the sentence is and that its source is unknown — several hands, no name. Nothing is invented, nothing is crossed out. The atlas backing is laid flat again over its many layers.

Henry writes on the source line: the caption, and beside it 'source — unknown; passed through several hands, no name.' The what-line is full; the source line now carries a described absence rather than a guess. Nothing is entered where the author would be.

Two caption cards sit side by side on the exhibition board. The left is Peter's own draft for a dark route point: 「この道は、だれも通らなくなってから、ずっと灯りがつけている。だれのためだろう。」 The right is Sophie's rewrite: 「人通りの絶えた道を、今もなお静かに照らし続ける、一つの灯り。その温かな光は、道行く人の心をそっと包み込むかのようです。」 The right one reads beautifully and says nothing Peter said.

On the board Peter's caption stands mended — one verb form changed, the closing question 「だれのためだろう」 still there. Sophie's polished rewrite is folded to one side, kept but no longer the version on show. Nothing of his has been overwritten.

The change is split into two columns: an ERROR column holding only 「がつけている → がついている」, and a VOICE column holding the words and the question that must stay untouched — 「だれのためだろう」. Whichever the last attempt over-changed comes back for another try; what was kept correctly stays put.
